speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I desire to briefly call attention to the conditions at Sault Ste. Marie in reference to the administration of the alien labour law. I shall first quote an article from the 'Evening News,' published at Sault Ste. Marie, Michigan, and Sault Ste. Marie, Ontario, under date Wednesday, March 15, 1911.

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext:
Men say Newcomers are Getting the Pick. Dismissed Official was Old Employee and Popular.
Immigration Officials are asked to make
Overtures with Department to stay Influx.
As a protest against the dismissal of ' Jack' Wilson, foreman of the electrical engineers employed by the Lake Superior corporation, the entire staff of 22 struck yesterday, and have not yet returned to work. Wilson has been in the service of the corporation for a number of_ years and is popular among the
This morning twenty-six electricians employed by the Lake Superior Corporation in rail mili went on strike, alleging that the management had dispensed with the services of electrician, J. Wilson, yesterday without cause. It is not yet known to what extent the strike will affect the operations of the mill. Strikers have not yet shown any disposition to return to work.
This is only the culmination of a long series of grievances which have been in existence at the towns of Sault Ste. Marie and Steelton. These grievances both now and in past years have been due to the fact that the Canadian Alien Labour Law has been laxly administered if there has been any attempt to administer it at all, and by reason of the lax and gravely inefficient administration of that law at the Sault there have been hundreds of importations into the towns of Sault Ste. Marie and Steelton of Americans in violation of that Act to the displacement of the working men of Canada, who are thus deprived of their wages and the bread and butter of themselves and their families. This is not the first time I have had occasion to make complaints about the conditions at Sault- Ste. Marie and Steelton. I know of my personal* knowledge that the Labour Department has on record that there have been continued importations of labour men from the American side in violation of the Alien Labour Law, and that no proceedings whatever have been

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: taken by the Labour Department to check them. The Alien Labour Law, as I understand it, is both reciprocal and retaliatory; reciprocal in that it will admit imported labour upon the same conditions as the United States will admit imported labour from Canada, and retaliatory in that it prohibits and penalizes the importation of contract labour to the same extent as contract labour going into the United States' from Canada is penalized. Our Alien Labour Law professes to prohibit the importation of the sort of labourers who are coming in by hundreds to the towns of Sault Ste. Marie and Steelton and displacing Canadian workmen. The Minister of Labour knows because it has been on the records of his department and of this House for three years at least, that this is daily occurring, and three years ago a remedy was solemnly promised by the government. At the present moment this grievance is marked; it may be said that a crisis has arisen and the newspaper report which I have sent over to the Minister of Labour points to only a small amount of the dissatisfaction that exists. It is a pity that with an Act -on our statute-books which is apparently workable and for the enforcement of which the government has appointed an officer-I think I am right in that?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: On that point the hon. gentleman is mistaken.

Then, although three years ago it was shown beyond question that there had been steady and constant violations of the law the minister has not yet appointed an officer to enforce it. I gave him and his predecessor in office more credit for vigilance than they deserved. I regret the acknowledgment of the minister that after the promises and the pledges made by his predecessor in the Department of Labour no official has been appointed to administer the provisions of the Alien Labour Act. Let me refer the minister to the report of the proceedings of the House on July 6, 1908, where at page 12156 of ' Hansard ' for that year he will find the following petition:
To the Hon. the Minister of Labour, Ottawa.
The petition of the undersigned citizens of the town of Sault Ste. Marie, in the province of Ontario, most respectfully showeth:
1.	That by reason of close proximity to the
international boundary your petitioners are more than usually alive to the fact there is no rigid enforcement of the provisions of anv law in force in Canada to restrict the importation and employment of aliens, and that in consequence industries here suffer by the employment of foreign labour.	[DOT]
2.	That your petitioners are aware of, and will draw to your attention, the fact that across the border the law is rigidly enforced, and that on that side of the line drastic and prompt measures are taken to immediately deport any Canadian citizen who goes across

to look for work and that in that respect your petitioners believe that the powers of the United States customs and immigration officers are exceeded.
3.	That in the opinion of your petitioners the present Act is not capable of giving prompt and adequate remedy which will meet the conditions which your petitioners know to exist, and your petitioners believe that more drastic and less cumbrous legislation should be enacted so as to enable prompt action to be taken by way of deportation of any aliens or foreigners seeking to enter Canada to wcrk therein under contracts made out in Canada, and so as to meet the condition of the things and the methods in which the law in the United States is enforced against Canadians.
4.	Your petitioners further would draw to your attention that there is no immigration inspector or other officers located here whose duty it is to see that the provisions of the Act in force are enforced and the consequence is both from the nature of the Act itself and from its non-enforcement, that the Canadian workmen are not adequately protected against foreign labour.
5.	Your petitioners therefore pray:
I commend to the Minister of Labour (Mr. King) who at that period was not in charge of the department, the remarks which I had then the honour to make in support of that petition, and I also commend to him the answers of his predecessor in office, the Hon. -Eodolphe Lemieux, which are reported at page 12159 of the ' Hansard,' 1908. Speaking on July the 7th, 1908 -in answer to my remarks upon the subject-the Hon. Mr. Lemieux said:

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
I thank my hon. friend for bringing this matter up this evening. His remarks as they appear in 'Hansard' will serve me to-morrow as a brief for the Minister of Justice. It is true that practically the administration of the labour law is in the hands of the Minister of Labour, but when these cases are taken to the Attorney General of Canada, that is the Minister of Justice, he acts jointly with me. My hon. friend says we should have a law' similar in its effects to the law in the neighbouring republic. I believe in retaliatory measures, we should favour the doctrine of an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth.
These were the words of the present Postmaster General: ' Ay eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth.'

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: That, is Christian.

That is the Mosaic law as well as the law of the Postmaster General. During the same debate the Postmaster General used this language further:
I have no doubt the remarks of my hon. friend which have been made in a fair spirit will have weight. I shall communicate with the Minister of Justice and see what better provision can be made to render the law more pliable and more effective in protecting our own people against the alien labour.

That was on July 7, 1908, and here we had a direct and definite promise by a minister of the Crown that the remarks made to, and the grievances, and the petition, which were laid before the House in a fair spirit as he says, should form a brief for the Minister of Justice to take prompt action next day to render the law more effective in. protecting our own people against alien labour. I ask the Minister of Labour whether anything has been done to carry out the pledge of his predecessor thus solemnly made. Has there been any attempt to amend the alien labour law so as to make it more pliable, and so as to protect the Canadian working man, his wife and family from the terrible effects of the importation of alien labour to the town of Sault St. Marie or at any other point on the Canadian border.
My hon. friend himself admits that nothing whatever has been done in reply to that earnest petition to appoint an officer to enforce the provisions of the law. Why has that not been done? This is not a mere temporary grievance. It is a permanent grievance. It is one that has existed from day to day and from year to year since that time. There have been, I understand, constant importation's of labour in violation of the Alien Labour Law, which have been brought to the notice of the minister and the minister has done absolutely nothing. I am now asking what he proposes to do. Does he not think that after three years it is high time something should be done to carry out the pledge made by the hon. Postmaster General (Mr. Lemieux), then speaking as Minister of Labour, to render more efficient the protection of the workingmen of Sault Ste. Marie and Steelton and elsewhere along the border. The hon. Postmaster General then promised that he would have our labour law applied more effectively and made something else besides a law in name only. I have said that the labour laws in the two countries are either reciprocal or retaliatory. The Postmaster General takes the more drastic view. He says they must be considered as retaliatory and believes in the doctrine of an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth. Well, I believe in the application of that doctrine laid down by the Postmaster General. I believe he should put an end to the conditions that have existed since July, 1908, as appears by the clipping from a newspaper I have referred to. I say that our Alien Labour Law should be treated as retaliatory and why? Because the Alien Labour Law on the other side of the line is administered in that spirit. We have heard a great deal lately about reciprocity in trade products, but if there ever was an example to show how that reciprocity will work out in favour of the United
States against Canada, it will be found in the condition of things under the Alien Labour Law. We have the same law here as they have in the United States, the same reciprocity, and the same power of retaliation. How does our law work out? No attempt whatever is made to stop the importation of alien labour from the United States; but let a Canadian citizen go across the line in search of work, and he is promply arrested and detained and deported under the Alien Labour Law of that country. I have here a despatch from Hamilton of March 9, a Canadian press despatch:
Alfred Stiles, a well known cutter, who left this city last week to accept a position at Terre Haute, Ind., was stopped by immigration officers at Detroit, and sent back to Canada with a warning that if he set foot in the United States again within a year he would render himself liable to imprisonment.
If that is not retaliatory law I do not know what is. What I want is to have our law administered in the same spirit. But hundreds of Canadians have been displaced in the factories and workshops at Sault Ste. Marie and Steelton by Americans imported in violation of the Act, and no step3 were taken to have the aliens deported. It is now three years since this matter was brought to the attention of this House, and since the Minister of Labour solemnly promised a remedy. I earnestly commend it again to his attention and ask him to get to work and put in force our Alien Labour Law, even if it be necessary to appoint 20 officers in order to protect our Canadian wTorkingmen and their wives and families.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
I am obliged to my hon. friend for having brought up this matter if only because he has given occasion to make a little clearer what is the nature of the laws of this country respecting the entry into Canada of aliens. Frequently the Department of Labour is charged with being indifferent in the administration of our laws regarding the admission of aliens. This attack is made regardless altogether of the fact that the Department of Immigration and other departments of the government have also a great deal to do with this matter. In fact the greater part of the work of restricting the entry of aliens falls within the scope of the Department of the Interior, and the immigration officials. It is only that part of immigration which has to do with contract labour that comes within the purview of the Alien Labour Act. My hon. friend has said that at Sault Ste. Marie he does not think there is any inspector for the purpose of enforcing this law, and left the impression that the Department of Labour was indifferent in this matter. I may inform him that within the

last few weeks officers of the Immigration Department have been very active at Sault Ste. Marie in refusing admittance to a large number from the United States. My hon. colleague the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver) will be able to inform my hon. friend more particularly on that point; but I do happen to know that within recent days he has received complaints from the management of the company at Sault Ste. Marie about the rigid manner in which our laws are being enforced and admission refused to a large number who came from across the line. My hon. friend read an article from the ' Evening News,' of March 15, respecting the dismissal of one of the employees of the Sault Company. I shall just quote the words of that article, because on it my hon. friend has largely based the complaint he has made.
That is only a public illustration of what is taking place, and it does not necessarily apply to all the con;-' ditions that exist there.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
At any rate my hon. friend introduced his remarks by quoting this article, and it is as he says a public illustration. It is as follows:
As a protest against the dismissal of Jack Wilson, foreman of the electrical engineers employed by the Lake Superior Corporation, the entire staff of twenty-two struck and have not yet returned to work. Wilson has been in the service of the corporation for a number of years and is popular among the workers who regard him as an extremely capable official. In his stead Shumaker has been placed, and the ire of the men was raised in consequence.
I contend there is nothing in that article on which my hon. friend can found a, charge as to the laxity of administration of the Alien Labour Act. All it states is that an employee of many years service, who was popular with the men, was dismissed and somebody else put m his place, and the employees to show their resentment at his dismissal, had gone out on strike.
As respects the administration of the Alien Labour Act, my hon. friend will realize that there are two methods which might be employed. One would require the federal government to take action every time that Act was violated; the other would leave it in the hands of the parties themselves to take' immediate action. As the law stood originally, before any action could be taken, the assent of the Attorney General had to be obtained. A number of complaints were made that inasmuch as the Attorney General of the Dominion had to be consulted before the law could be put into motion, the delays were such as to render it practically ineffective.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour

speechtext: Has the minister not received reports and complaints from Sault Ste. Marie and Steelton that the provisions of the Act had been violated.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
I shall answer that in a< moment. Complaints were made that ini as much as parties were obliged to send their complaints to Ottawa there was too much delay, and the labour organizations, particularly of British Columbia, which were specially interested, asked that the law should be so amended as to render it unnecessary for the workingmen to come to Ottawa for redress. That seemed very reasonable, and in 1901 the law was am 'tided in such a way that those who complained of its violation could make their complaint either before the Attorney General of the province, or a judge of the comity court, and, on getting the consent of either, could take immediate action. I would like to read the section of the law in that particular. In the first place, the clause which sets out the offence in the broadest terms, as follows:
It shall be unlawful for any person, company, partnership or corporation, in any manner to prepay the transportation or in any way to assist, encourage or solicit the importation or immigration of any aliens or foreigners into Canada, under contract or agreement, parole or special, express or implied, made previous to the importation or immigration of such alien or foreigner, to perform labour or service of any kind in Canada.
The penalty fixed for the violation of the section is a fine not exceeding $1,000, and not less than $50, which amount may be ' sued for and recovered as a debt,' or

Such sum may also, with the written consent	of a judge of a superior
county court, be recovered upon summary conviction before any judge of a county court, being a justice of the peace or any judge of the sessions of the peace, recorder, police magistrate or stipendiary magistrate, or any functionary, tribunal or person invested by the proper legislative authority with power to do alone such acts as are usually required to be done by two or more justices of the peace, and, when recovered, shall be paid to the Minister of Finance.
In other words, the provisions of the law have been made such that any party, anywhere in the Dominion who feels that this the broad clause which I have read is being violated can immediately take action of his own initiative to secure the enforcement of the provision. And not only is that the law, but there is a further provision which says that in the event of it being shown that the law has been violated and a fine imposed, the party who has been instrumental in bringing about the prosecution may be awarded a part of the fine imposed. I have here a communication received only a few days ago from Judge
55:>3

Fitch, Of the District of Rainy River, not far from where my hon. friend (Mr. Boyce) resides:
Quite a long way.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Of course, the distances are considerable in this country. Judge Fitch says:
I to-day found the Johnson-Carey Company, railroad contractors, guilty of a breach of the Alien Labour Law and fined them $500. From the evidence, this company has not been paying any attention to this Act, but I do not imagine we will have much more trouble in the future. I would be obliged if you would advise me as to the disposition of the fine. Will it be paid to the clerk of the peace or to the Dominion government? I would recommend that the informant, Ed. Oleson, who laid the information and hired a solicitor, should receive $200.
As Minister of Labour, having authority under the Act so to do, I have advised the Minister of Finance that, under the circumstances, half of this penalty-a greater amount than that named by the judge himself-should be paid to the informer. And, I think, as the judge has stated, that this company, having learned what the law is and having seen that it is possible for any person to put it in force in a summary manner, will be careful to observe the law in the future. This is only one of a number of cases. I have here quite a number of similar communications received during past years from magistrates and others informing the department of convictions under the Act. The department has, in every case, recommended payment to the informant part of the penalty imposed as a result of the conviction which he has been instrumental in obtaining. I think that my hon. friend (Mr. Boyce), if he reflects.'will feel that, on the whole, this is a more effective way of securing compliance with the provisions of the Act than for this government to have one or trvo officers whose business it is to watch possible violations of the law along a border of between three and four thousand miles between the Atlantic and the Pacific.
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: There is a difference of opinion-
The hon. gentleman's (Mr. King's) predecessor in office admitted that it was not so. I quoted the speech the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lemieux) made on July 7, 1908.

speechtext: Can. the hon. minister (Mr King) tell me from whom the communication was received to-day?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
From Mr. Denman, correspondent at Sault Ste Marie of the Labour Gazette 

'riling on behalf of others. A reply is being sent to Mr. Denman explaining the procedure and asking him to inform the parties that any one who lays information against a violator of the Act and obtains a conviction will be entitled to one-half the penalty which may be imposed. I think that if my hon. friend (Mr. Boyce) will take into account the fact that it is only that part which has to do with contract labour that is administered by my department, while the general law respecting immigration comes under the Department of Immigration and has regard also to the effective means being taken by the Department of Immigration to administer its part of the law, he will find that there is really no ground of complaint.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: PUBLIC HEALTH - CONDITIONS AT GROSSE ISLE.
PUBLIC HEALTH - CONDITIONS AT GROSSE ISLE.
speechtext:
I desire to call the attention of the government to a matter of importance-I think it may be said, of urgent importance. I have a memorandum here from a gentleman of very high reputation in the country, well known to every member of the government, and, I think, to almost every member of the House. It is as follows:
It is considered by gentlemen whose opinion is entitled to respect that dangerous conditions exist in the quarantine station at Grosse Isle. In view of the possible outbreak of a fresh cholera epidemic in Europe, they say there is cause for alarm in view of the fact that last autumn a cholera case was allowed to pass the quarantine station and reach Quebec. The facilities at Grosse Isle do not permit proper inspection to be made there. If a ship arrived with a case of contagious disease on board the victims have to be taken ashore in a small tug and all sorts of dangers are likely to result. Considering the enormous expenditure for useless wharfs, why is not the wharf at Grosse Isle extended so as to allow ocean steamships to approach and discharge their passengers?
However that may be, certainly, I think this should not be allowed to pass without serious attention from the government. I recollect that last year there was some rumour about a cholera patient arriving and being allowed to go as far as Quebec or some such point. If that occurred in one case, it might possibly occur again. I hope the government will take pains to consider what is stated here and provide a barrier against the danger referred to.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
In view of the alarming reports presented by Dr. Hodgetts with regard to the unsanitary condition of the city of Ottawa, I would like to know something more as to the authority under which he was acting-it seems he is acting under the Conservation Commission-according to what principles he is. acting, and when he was induced to take action. I have referred to this question once before, many -weeks Mr. MARTIN (Regina).
ago, from information that I had received, when I spoke pretty strong on the subject. I have watched the action of those who ought to be interested, and who I think are largely responsible, and it has seemed to me as a medical man that very little was being done which ought to be done to improve the unsanitary condition of the city of Ottawa, and to protect the health and lives of the members who, for the time being, reside here, and of the citizens as well. I said at that time, sipeaking as a medical man, that I had reason to believe that the medical health officer was absolutely useless, and that there was imminent danger to the health and the lives of the people of this city in consequence. I said that because of the number of people who live temporarily in Ottawa during the session of parliament, I thought it was imperative on the government to take some action, to insist upon the city doing its duty, and that some constituted authority ought to be empowered to take the work in hand, and do that which the city authorities were failing to do. I based my argument for this upon the ground that the Dominion government are spending large sums of money in the city of Otawa to ornament it, and to help improve the city generally, and from certain supplies furnished to the country, one of which was a supply of water for these buildings and for needs in event of fire. I was told then that it was not the duty of the government to act, that they had nothing to do with the matter, and iperhaps in one way they had not. But at any irate, week after week has passed, during which hundreds of cases of typhoid fever have developed, accompanied with many deaths, and we have gone so far as to make an analysis of the water two or three times, which analysis has disclosed the fact that the city water is unhealthy, which must be known by every person without an analysis. The very fact that so many cases of disease have started up, and could be traced to no other source, was strong presumptive evidence that the water was the source of the trouble. In the ' Citizen of this morning I find a report by Dr. Hodgetts, in which he says:
Acting on the reports made by the officers now engaged in the work of the collection of information for the Commission of Conservation, I have personally visited some of the premises reported to be in an unsanitary state. I find conditions existing in some of the>
homes where privy pits are in use to be of such a disgraceful character as to warrant my drawing your immediate attention to thei same. They are a menace to the persons living in the immediate vicinity and, if allowed to continue, the untreated excreta of typhoid patients which have been deposited in these sometimes overlooked privies and, in some

instances, even thrown upon the ground, cannot fail to be a source of infection and will, with the approach of milder weather, prove a ready means of spreading the disease.
Where such a relic of medievalism (privy pit) is in use and becomes the receptacle of the excreta of a typhoid fever patient, it is imperative there should be thorough and careful disinfection of the contents; and for this purpose the health department should exercise the greatest vigilance by systematically performing the necessary services, for if left to the individual householder, it is found the work is never properly performed.
The conditions to which your attention is directed are such as to call for immediate action by yourself and the local Board of Health.	,
He goes on to give a list of houses.
Accompanying this communication is a list of houses in which typhoid fever has been reported and where the officers of the commission find privy pits in use. Similar lists will be sent you from time to time. A copy of this letter is being forwarded to His Worship, Mayor Hopewell.
The list of houses mentioned contains fifteen names on Stirling, Lauretta, St. Patrick, St. Andrew, Church, Water, Victoria, LeBreton, Murton and Wellington streets. The second letter, dated March 13, was as follows:-
Having examined a portion of that section of the city situated along Cave creek in order to ascertain the sanitary conditions, I am of the opinion it is necessary that immediate attention should be given the same.
Instances are many where outside closets are discharging directly into the creek, and m one case the back portion of the house is built over the creek, and all the excremental matter is deposited in the creek down an outside closet. Prom this house the creek flows under other houses in process of construction.
Again, the creek has overflowed into back yards carrying sewage -with it, ancj in the floor of a shed of one house I found several inches of frozen sewage with masses of human excreta embedded therein. A more disgusting sight I have never seen in any city; and with the advent of spring the condition will not improve.
As it is now, Cave creek is simply a sewer of the crudest and most dangerous type, and drastic measures should be adapted forthwith whereby its pollution will be prevented.
I find that water is being taken from Lazy bay at a point not far distant from the month of Cave creek and sold to residents in the vicinity. If the sale extends to residents within the city limits, the practice should lie prohibited.
It is possible you are already aware of the condition 'indicated above through your sanitary inspectors.
He goes on to sneak of the conditions in other respects. Now when we know that that condition has continued for weeks in the city of Ottawa, which has nominally a hoard of health and a medical inspector at the head of it, and when attention has heen pointedly drawn to the condition
through the press of Ottawa day after day, and week after week, and that up to the last few days nothing has been done, the situation seems to me beyond comprehension. I think the government has been very remiss, their attention having been drawn to it over and over again, and they have practically said, what can we do?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: This government or the government of Ontario?

The government of the Dominion right where we are located at the present time, and which is paying to the city a large amount of money to help defray the expenses of the city, to adorn it, and to make it more healthy and attractive than it is and for the water supplied. This is the place where we have our Inland Revenue Department, where we have our analytical chemists, where we have our experimental farm, where we have professional men who are specially qualified to look into thepe things, and to make a report to the government. This is the city where the Dominion government has so much at stake, with two or three thousand civil servants employed doing the work of the country, and all dependent upon the government for their subsistence, and the government, which has entirely neglected these things, is in my judgment not doing their full duty, and we are right in drawing attention to it. I want to ask under what authority, or by what means, or under whose instructions, Dr. Hodgetts is acting? I am told that it is under the authority of the Conservation Commission. I did not know whether the Conservation Commission had authority delegated to them to institute such an inquiry or appoint a medical inspector to inspect the city. If it is done under the Conservation Commission, the Conservation Commission is under the government and the Conservation Commission has been in existence ever since the commencement of the session of parliament. Why could not the government have acted earlier. Why could they not have taken the action^ that they have done within the last few days, six o>r ten weeks ago? It was quite apparent then, as it is to-day, that something was wrong, that there was practically no board of health of any Value or medical health officer worthy of the name.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: Whose fault is that? Are they not appointed by the Ontario government?

It is the fault of the city council. They have the power and duty to appoint this local board of health, and to see that the local board is doing its duty. But, with the fact made evident to us that

the board is not doing its duty, is it not strange that the government has taken no action until within the last few days. I 'would like to know under what authority they are acting now, how they propose to carry on the inquiry that is taking place, and what they propose to do regarding it.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) has asked a question with regard to the authority of Dr. Hod-getts, and by whom he has been appointed. Dr. Hodgetts is in the employ of the Conservation Commission. One of the objects that the Conservation Commission has to deal with is the health of the people, but I understand that under the law his work will be confined to making investigations into the public health and giving advice. I presume that is what he is doing in this case. I do not understand that he would have any authority to carry his recommendations into effect. I understand that that is a matter entirely for the local board of health. My hon. friend sought to find fault with the government because we had not taken action earlier. He has read a long report as to the condition of different houses and privies in various places in the city of Ottawa. This government has no power over that. It is a matter entirely for the local authorities.
Had the government not power to appoint Dr. Hodgetts two months ago?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: Dr. Hodgetts is simply going to investigate, that is all.
That is a valuable part of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
He cannot give orders; he cannot have his recommendations carried out. He has no authority over the matter; all he can do is to investigate and advise, and that, I take it, is what he is doing. I do not know how it is in the province of Ontario, because I have not read the Health Act, but in the province of New Brunswick, whose Health Act is largely the same as the Ontario Act, the appointment of the boards of health rests to a very considerable extent with the provincial government. They appoint the provincial board of health and the provincial board has the control over the local boards of health. I think that my hon. friend, instead of finding fault with this government, if he wanted to find fault with anybody, would perhaps have done better if he had sent a communication to the government of Ontario, urging that they should see that their authorities on the provincial board of health took active measures to see that the necessary steps were taken in the city of Ottawa. My hon. friend says that the local board of health is useless. Well, we have no control over the local board of health, Mr. SPROULE.
no power to interfere with it in any way. It is very true that the government is a large consumer of water, just the same as the citizens of Ottawa are large consumers of water. There is nothing I see that we could do immediately which would ensure ta better water supply than we have. To get *another source of water supply for the city of Ottawa would cost a great deal of money. That is for the local authorities to attend to. I would suppose that they would feel that it would be right to tax the people for the purpose of going to any reasonable expense in order to get a pure and good supply of water, but that is not something that the government can do. The Finance Minister was questioned as to the speech delivered by President Taft, at Atlanta, especially to the following extract:
When we entered upon these negotiations, I asked the Secretary of State and his commissioners to offer free trade in everything, but this Canada could not grant us, because she has a protective system and she was afraid of the competition of our better-organized industries.
To this the Minister of Finance replied;
That statement may be entirely correct, and I have no doubt is, as to the instructions that the President gave to his officials. But as to what actually occurred in the conference, the matter did not advance to a position which would enable these gentlemen to make such a formal offer in that way. At the very earliest stage in the negotiations we certainly gave them to understand that we could not undertake to have any free trade in manu factnres, speaking generally.

This is the position of the government. We have undertaken to have reciprocity in natural products, not in manufactured products. At the present time our policy is before the House to have reciprocity in natural products, and I shall be very glad if we have the assistance of our friends that far in favour of the farmers. I doubt very much if we will, but we will see what we will do afterwards.

I am afraid the Prime Minister missed the meaning of my hon. friend's question. A supporter of my right hon. friend goes to a rural constituency and says he has the authority of the Prime Minister, and the Minister of Finance to make that definite statement. What my hon. friend wants to know is whether the member was authorized by the Prime Minister or Finance Minister to make that statement. Before explaining the details of this vote, I would like to be permitted to place before the committee ^some facts and figures in regard to the work done under this vote during the past and previous years. As the committee is aware, the administration of Dominion lands has a very important influence upon the increase of population and of the productive wealth of Canada. Therefore, it is a matter of great interest to the country to know the results which have been reached by the expenditure of this money. I am sure the committee will be gratified to know that under the vote for Dominion lands during the calendar year 1910, there was the largest amount of land settlement in the prairie provinces that has ever taken place in the history of Canada. The number of individual entries for land were 52,072, besides 18,352 pre-emption entries. In all therefore, there were taken 70,424 separate entries for land. These 70,000 entries represented a total area of 11,617,600 acres. It may interest the committee to know that the amount of land in the three prairie provinces which passed to individuals last year on conditions of residence and cultivation, was almost equal to the total area of the 23 countries which constituted the western peninsula of Ontario, an area of 11,840,000 acres. It may be of further interest to know that in this corresponding area in the western peninsula of Ontario, there was, at the census of 1901, a population of 1,313,000 people, a little short of one-fourth of the total population of the Dominion at that time. That is to say, under the operation of the Dominion Lands Branch of the Interior Department last year, an area of land passed into the hands of individuals on conditions of residence and cultivation, equal to the 23 counties constituting the western peninsula of Ontario, including York and Simcoe.
This area,_ judged by the standard of the western peninsula of Ontario, is capable of supporting at any rate over a million and a quarter of people. The conditions of cultivation which are attached to the entries of -which I spoke, without the fulfilment of which conditions the titie to the land cannot pass to the individual, applied to 2,500,000 acres, that is to say the government of Canada entered into contracts with 52,072 people last year to bring under cultivation 2,517,020 acres of land, the condition being that the title should not pass unless that amount of land was cultivated. It may further interest the committee to know that this area of cultivation under contract is very nearly double the total area of the province of Prince Edward Island. Last year there was put under contract to cultivate 2,517,020 acres of land while the total 1751
land area of Prince Edward Island is 1,397,760 acres.
The rapidity of the increase of settlement is also, I assume, a matter of some interest. While the individuals making entry during 1910 were 52,072, in the year 1909 the individuals making entry were 40,408. Five years ago the number of individuals making entry was 34,503; five years before that, in 1900, it was 7,764 and five years before that, in 1895, it was 2,326. In the three periods of five years each the number of entries has practically doubled in each period and during the last period, while the number of entries has not been actually doubled, the amount of land entered for has been more than doubled and the amount of cultivation contracted for has increased fourfold.
It may also be of interest to the committee to be informed as to the result following the passage of the Land Bill of 1908. which placed at the disposal of homestead settlers all the land not then alienated in these prairie provinces without regard to whether it was comprised within odd or even numbered sections. By the Act of 1908 the lands which had been held under reservation for the purpose of aid to railways or such other purpose as might be through fit were made available to homestead settlement without distinction of number or place.
That was not in the railway belt?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Not in the railway belt of British Columbia. I am not speaking of that; I am speaking entirely of the three prairie provinces. That feature of the Bill of 1908 was that in a certain area of Saskatchewan and Alberta a pre-emption privilege was allowed for reasons which were set forth at that time. Within that area a homesteader was entitled, when entering for his free homestead, to enter also for an adjoining quarter-section as a preemption upon which he should pay a price, and upon which lie would do cultivation duties and in regard to which he had to establish residence. I need not perhaps repeat that the area of country extending, roughly speaking, for a distance of 400 miles along the main line of the Canadian Pacific railway between Moosejaw and Calgary -I do not wish to be understood as saying extending from Moosejaw to Calgary, but for a distance extending 400 miles along the railway between these two points-up to the passage of the Bill of 1908, contained very little settlement. For one reason or another it had not proved attractive to settlers. I am not able to give the number of homesteaders who were settled within that area up to that time, but those who are familiar with the conditions will, I am

sure, agree with me that the number, as compared with the area under consideration, was comparatively small. Since the adoption of the principle of pre-emption which took effect the 1st September, 1908, there have been taken -within that area, as the result of the provision of the Act of that date, 46,066 pre-emptions representing a total area of 7,370,560 acres upon which, in order to earn title, cultivation was required amounting to 2,303,300 acres. It may be of interest to the committee to know that the area taken in pre-em-tions since the 1st September, 1908, in a district which up to that time had not been considered favourable by settlers, is more than equal to the total area of that part of the province of Quebec which lies south of the St. Lawrence river extending from the western limit of the province to a I oint south of the city of Quebec, containing altogether twenty-two counties. In a little over two years undeT the pre-emption provision of the law of 1908 an area of land was taken up in that particular part of the northwest which hitherto had not been considered attractive to settlers equal to twenty-two counties of the province of Quebec, and' I think I am safe in saying the twenty-two counties in the province of Quebec which contain the greater part of the presently occupied agricultural area, at any rate, that which is most densely peopled and most profitably worked. The area of the twenty-two counties is 6,508,000 acres, as compared with 7,370,560 acres taken under pre-emption and entry since September 1, 1908. In connection with these pre-emption entries there were taken of course an equal number, 46,066 of homestead entries. Some of the homestead entries had already been taken, but there were taken after the first of September, 1908, in connection with the pre-emption entries not less than 46,000 homesteads representing an area of 6,400,000 acres, and calling for cultivation to the amount of 1,200000 acres. That is to say in that one area of the Northwest under the special provision of the Act of 1908, an area of land has passed to actual settlers under conditions of residence and cultivation that is more than double the total area of the twenty-two counties of the province of Quebec which contain the major portion of the population of that province.
Another feature of the Act of 1908 which was looked upon with some doubt by a number of the members of this House was the purchased homestead provision. Under this provision a man who had exhausted his homestead right became entitled to acquire 160 acres of land within the preemption area under conditions of residence and cultivation equal to those required in the case of an ordinary homestead, and in addition he was required to pay the Mr. OLIVER.
sum of $3 an acre. It was suggested at the time by those who were opposed to this provision that to allow the settler to acquire an additional homestead at such a low price would tend to unsettle the conditions existing throughout the greater part of the prairie country. It was declared by a gentleman who had some right to speak with authority, a member representing a constituency in the province of Manitoba, that such a privilege would be bound to be a serious detriment to the already settled sections of the country. However, the provision was agreed to and went into effect with this result:	While 46,066 preemptions were taken, only 3,726 purchased homesteads were taken, an area of 596,160 acres, calling for cultivation to the1 amount of 186,300 acres. The fears which were expressed at the time of the injurious effect of this provision have not been realized. The acquirement of a matter of 3,726 purchased homesteads in the pre-emption aTea has not injuriously disturbed existing conditions of settlement in the older settled portions of the prairie provinces, while it has at the same time afforded opportunity to the man who had already exhausted his homestead right, and for one reason or another desired to take another chance at fortune, an opportunity on reasonable terms and was availed of in 3,726 cases. The operation of the provision, I think, justified its adoption by the House, and has not at all borne out the objections that were urged against it.

How many of those 3,726 purchased homesteads were acquired by men who, having already acquired homesteads, say in Manitoba, had perhaps without a due appreciation of the law, fraudulently acquired new homesteads in other provinces by taking what were really false oaths, as subsequently ascertained by the officials of the department.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
None of the 3,726 purchased homesteads would come into the class mentioned because the man who had exhausted his homestead right by coming into the purchased homestead area had the right to take another homestead under these conditions. The cases mentioned by my hon. friend are not within the law, arid are not included within this number. They are cases where men acquired their homesteads and afterwards illegally acquired other homesteads not in the pre-emption area, and having acquired the second homesteads illegally, thereby placed themselves under penalty of the law. In many of these cases we have taken a lenient view, and have sometimes cancelled the fraudulent entry, and sold them the land at a price which would take away the clean profit that they would have made if they had got the land on their first fraudulent entry. Within the

pre-emption area the price at which the land can be purchased is $3 an acre. When we find a man who has secured fraudulent entry outside the purchase homestead area we charge him a price over $3, sometimes $4, or sometimes more. In no case that I know of have we demanded a price on the actual valuation of the land. We may have been more lenient than we should, but we cannot be accused of having dealt unfairly by these people. Some of them possibly may have had a misunderstanding, but whether or not we are inclined to deal leniently rather than harshly with them. Of course, if a plan puts himself within reach of the criminal law he takes his chances, and if he is punished he has no ground of complaint.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: This department has nothing to do with the administration of criminal law. In some cases prosecutions have been entered under the criminal law, which is under the administration of the province. Our compromise with any man in regard to the ownership of the land does not relieve him from the operation of the criminal law if any one chooses to invoke it against him.
It might mitigate the offence.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It might, but we have nothing to do with the criminal aspect of it.

Some years ago a man who had had a homestead in Manitoba asked, through the legal column of the Winnipeg ' Free Press ', the Liberal organ, whether he could take a homestead in one of the western provinces, and the answer was that under the law he had a perfect right to take a homestead in Saskatchewan or Alberta after having taken one in Manitoba. The minister knows as well as I do that the farmers of the Northwest, particularly the pioneers, have not much time to read the newspapers; they do not know anything about the quibbles of the law, and when they hear that the government organ gives such advice, and when they act upon it, they certainly ought to be treated as leniently as possible. Now,
there is no doubt that in many cases where perjury lias been committed and a second homestead taken or it may be a third, the government has been very lenient and has taken care that certain individuals should have the privilege of buying these homesteads at prices below the real value. I believe in that leniency myself, but I point out to the minister that I know of three cases in my own constituency, and about them I have spoken to the minister, where the men are the worst Tories or the best Tories, just from the point of view you look at it, and who are unfortunate enough to be illiterate, but who relied absolutely upon what was expounded as the policy of this government in the Winnipeg ' Free Press ', and perjured themselves it is true -I do not excuse that for a moment,-but thinking they had to comply with some quibble or some phraseology to get what they thought was their right, they did apply for a second homestead. These three men are languishing in jail to-day, and at the same time I could name to the minister off hand a dozen staunch Liberals who have committed the same perjury, but who to-day are freemen and have their homesteads and have been granted their patents. I do not wish to mention the name of any man who has not the right to come here and answer me, but I say this is a fact, and I say it is absolutely unfair to give one man, because he is a Liberal and has a political pull with some one in this House, rights and privileges that are not extended to the Conservatives who support me. I do not believe for a moment that the Minister of the Interior knows of these facts; I think he is too big to do anything of the kind. I do not want to throw a bouquet at him by any means, but I can tell him that his department is and always has been absolutely rotten in that particular regard, and I want him to know it. I ask him to guide himself by that knowledge.
I will hand to him if he asks for them the names and he may rest assured that the facts are as I state them. I have three men languishing in jail for doing what dozens of Liberal heelers and government supporters have done in the last ten or fifteen years in the Northwest, and who are to-day freemen. These men are in jail because they would not support my opponent last election; there is no other reason. The man who sent the information tb the department against them is the man who put in a petition against me and accused me of every crime in the calendar. As was ably said by the Minister of Justice to-day, the fact is that a man who has been chosen by the people of his constituency is open to some scallawag getting uf>
and accusing him of every crime in the calendar, and there is no possible law by which that individual can be punished. This man to whom I refer, who petitioned

against me, tried time and time again in the office in Dauphin to break the laws and perjure himself and get a second homestead, but the officers of the Interior Department there knew him; they knew the circumstances, and they would not permit such an infraction of the law. The same man went to Saskatchewan and entered for a homestead, stayed there for a year or two, and perjured himself to the knowledge of the Minister of the Interior, or at least of his department, and after a year pr two his homestead was taken away from him. Was he prosecuted for perjury? Not much. He was too good a Liberal; he was the petitioner against my election.
Who is this man?

I shall not mention his name. I want to appeal to the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver) to put in practice what the hon. member for Victoria and Haliburton has brought to his attention. While leniency is -a good thing, and we all approve of it, especially where there is illiteracy and want of knowledge, let that leniency not be onesided, let it be fair, let the poor, illiterate Tories-and there are some illiterate Tories, but jjot as many as there are Liberals-get a fighting chance to make good. I could go on and tell the minister about two of those cases in Dauphin-boys who hardly can write their names-who were told by the Liberals that the ' Free Press ' said that they could go and do this if they went into another province. They went and did it and are now in jail. One is an old man married to an invalid wife, a bedridden woman, with no money and nothing to keep her except the charity of the people. The other is the son, the sole support of his parents, and he is in jail. Why? Because he is a Tory and voted against Burrows-nothing else.
I can hardly believe that any such state of affairs exists such as my hon. friend depicts.
You ought to know.

I cannot believe that any man is treated by the Department of the Interior in a different way, in any shape or form, because he is a Liberal. During the five or six years that I was in charge of that land department, I never knew of a case of that kind. I have now been a member of this House for seven years and have had a good many complaints to make to the Minister of the Interior for being so absolutely strict in carrying out the .regulations in such an arbitrary manner-not giving away a little, not giving little concessions to settlers that in my judgment should be given. But I can say this, that I have never in one single instance in my own constituency, in the last seven years, got one bit of consideration for any one Mr. CAMPBELL.
Liberal or Conservative, or for any Liberal more than Conservative, in any shape or form, and I do not believe that any such partiality exists in the west to-day.
I do not believe that any Liberal in any part of the country can get any consideration which is not coming to him fairly, because I have not been able to get anything for any of my friends, Liberal or Conservative, in the way of extension of time or any little considerations of that kind.
That must have been a sad disappointment.

In some cases it has been, because there are cases in which I think consideration might be given to the settler and nobody would be hurt. But I can say, absolutely, that not in a single case has anything been given a Liberal in my constituency that would not be given a 'Conservative.

I wish to add my endorsa-tion to what my hon. friend from Assini-boia (Mr. Turriff) has said. The hon. member for Dauphin has stated that homesteaders are treated differently, according to their political views and opinions. Well, I think I have had as much to do in the matter of corresponding with the department in behalf of homesteaders as my hon. friend from Dauphin (Mr. Campbell) and probably somewhat more in recent years- since, at least, the present Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver) has had charge of that department. Some seven or eight years ago the Humboldt constituency had hardly any homesteaders, hardly any people at all. At present there are many thousands of homesteaders in that constituency, and I have never known one single case in which a man's political affiliations were taken into consideration, so far as his treatment by the Minister of the Interior or the Department of the Interior is concerned. I have the same complaint to make as my hon. friend from Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff), and that is that sometimes the regulations of the department are administered too strictly. I have also the complaint to make that, in my judgment, some of those regulations are in themselves too severe. In some instances they go possibly beyond the spirit and intent of the Dominion Lands Act. But I have this to say, in justice to the Minister of the Interior and his department, that I have never known one case in which a man got consideration because he was a Liberal or was refused consideration because he .was a Conservative. I have written the Department of the Interior in the matter of '.dealing with homesteads, not about a few cases, but about hundreds of cases, and I 'do not know that any man from the west has had a larger correspondence along this line than I have had. That is due simply

to the tact that Humboldt constituency has been actively homesteaded during the time I have resided in it; and in all that time, in no instance, to my knowledge, has any man been given any more consideration because he was a Liberal than he would have been given if he had been a Conservative. I want to say further, that, in my opinion, it is not a fair statement to make in this House, without sufficient and positive proof, that any man is refused consideration because he is a Conservative. There may be occasions when my hon. friend thinks Conservatives were hardly dealt Svith by the department; but in such cases it was not because they were Conservatives but because they broke the law. My hon. friend tells us of a man who had gone to jail, but he gave himself the reason. It was because he had perjured himself.
What about the other ones? Some got off.

The hon. member for Dauphin is a public man, he was elected as a representative of his constituency and as a representative of the people of Canada. If he knows of any case where men, who are not in jail, ought to be in jail-
The minister knows it and admits it.
They were tried and acquitted.
Never acquitted.

If my hon. friend knows of men who ought to be in jail and are not, who have committed crimes for which they should be in jail, it is his duty as a public man to lay that information before the department. And I will guarantee that, inside of twenty-four hours, the Minister of the Interior will institute an investigation and will carry out the spirit and the letter of the law.
Oh, oh.
My hon. friends opposite should not be too severe on the officials of the department or the department itself.

I was not either, was
1?
It is known that my hon. friend has even taken steps himself, on certain occasions, to lead even officials to do what was not in the best interest of the country.
My hon. friend is a liar, absolutely a liar.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. gentleman (Mr. Campbell) will realize that that language is not allowed. It will be necessary for him to withdraw those words.
I rise to a point of order.
I call him a liar, and 1 refuse to take it back.
I rise to a point of order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I do not think I can hear any other point of order than the oni! I have raised.
He had better talk of his honesty? Where is the capital of Saskatchewan? What does it cost to vote fcr it?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Dauphin will realize, I am sure, that he has spoken hastily, and also that his words are not parliamentary. I think that will be sufficient to cause him to withdraw them.

But, previous to that point of order there is one which the Chair did not raise. The hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Neely), was out of order in making the statements he did concerning the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Campbell), and it is his place first to withdraw his declaration.
What I said goes. He is absolutely a liar. But if it is not par liamentary, I take the word back. But he is absolutely a liar.
Order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is distinctly out of order. Such a breach of order must be
Order, order.
I will not take a word back, he is a liar, first, last, and all the time.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Inasmuch as the hon. member has refused to withdraw, unless he will, even at this moment withdraw, it will be my duty to report the matter to the House for such action as it deems proper and desirable. I will still give him an opportunity to withdraw, for he, himself, must realize very clearly how unparliamentary his expression is.
It is a hard task, Mr. Chairman, to withdraw something that is absolutely true.
That is no withdrawal.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member must obey the rule and withdraw the expression.
I will withdraw the expression, at your order, Mr. Chairman.
Now, you had better make that man withdraw-
Order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If there is a point of order with regard to any previous expression, let the hon. member state the point of order, and I will hear it.

I raised the point of order. The hon. member for Humboldt, in charging the hon. member for Dauphin with seeking to induce an officer of the Crown, an officer in the service of this government, to perform an illegal and criminal act, is unparliamentary.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I did not understand the hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Neely) to use the terms attributed to him by the hon. member for Victoria and Haliburton (Mr. Hughes). Had I understood so, I would have called the hon. member to order myself. But, the point of order having been raised and the charge made that these words were used, I will allow the hon. member for Humboldt to state whether they were correctly understood or not, and to make his explanation.
I did not use those words. I said, and I repeat what I said, that the hon. member for Dauphin himself-
Did he sell the capital of Saskatchewan?
My hon. friend (Mr. Hughes) perhaps has something to say. I will give him an opportunity to say it. I am not cowardly enough to make insinuations-
Order, order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. gentleman (Mr. Neely) must confine himself, at this time, to an explanation of the point of order.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Hughes) is interrupting me while I make my statement.
Mr. Chairman, why don't you call this gentleman to order?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I have not realized that any breach of order has been made.
I rise to a point of order. Do you, Mr. Chairman, deem the word ' cowardly ' within the rules of debate in this House?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I have not heard the word ' cowardly ' as attached to the hon. member for Victoria and Halibnr-ton.	.

I said I was not cowardly enough to make insinuations across the floor of this House. If I have anything to say to any man, I will not be like some hon. members, but will make my statements openly and plainly. I only ask that any man in this House who has anything Mr. SCHAFFNER.
to say about me shall say it openly-let
him make a statement and then we will be able to deal with the matter. Now I did not say my hon. friend from Dauphin had compelled any official to do any illegal act. I said that my hon. friend from Dauphin had made the admission or the statement-
That is absolutely false.
Excuse me, you do not know what I was going to say yet.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. gentleman should at least wait until the statement is completed.

That in connection with a certain transaction, a firm with which my hon. friend was identified in connection with a certain transaction by which that firm obtained a grazing lease-I will put my statement plainly-in the Northwest- that it cost that firm a certain amount in order to induce an official of the department to obtain this grazing lease from the department.
Where do I come in?
I have a stenographic report in which the hon. member for Dauphin, in his election campaign, made that statement.
Mr. Chairman, you have just heard the statement he has made, that he has a stenographic report. I demand that here and now. I believe his statement

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. gentleman will have an opportunity to do that, but the statement is not completeu. I will ask the hon. member for Humboldt to understand that a point of order was raised with regard to certain expressions that he used. He has the right to explain, but I think an elaborate discussion of some other circumstances would hardly be in order. I will ask him to make his explanation as concisely as possible.

I am not making an elaborate explanation. I am explaining that I did not make the statement that the hon. member for Dauphin, or some other hon. gentleman said I did, and on which they raise the point of order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If that be the case, if the hon. member for Humboldt denies having used the words attributed to him by the hon. member for Victoria and Haliburton, his denial must, under the rules of the House, be accepted. In that case, unless another point of order is raised, the hon. member may proceed.

As I understood the remarks of this gentleman from Humboldt, they were to the effect that I had admitted

doing something that was illegal and wrong. That is what I understood. My protest was unparliamentary, and, Mr. Chairman, you know that I am always ready to express my regret to you for falling from grace. When I say that, I say all that is to be said. No man alive-that has been my religion- no man alive can come to my face and say to me: You did a mean thing or a crooked thing. That is my religion. And this member from Humboldt cannot do it anywhere outside of this House, and he can't get Jim Jeffries to do it outside of this House, but I will give them some of the fairest sport they ever had. Is it a fair thing that a creature of circumstances like the member for Humboldt-if that language is parliamentary-can get up and say here under your protection something that he cannot say anywhere else in God's wide world? What he said is absolutely, first, and all the time, false. It was the ' Free Press, the Liberal newspaper of Ottawa
I rise to a point of order, I have the floor.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think the point of order is correct. The hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Campbell), rose to the point of order, the point of order has not been stated explicitly, and if he will explain the point of order I will listen to him.	1

I will state it again. The hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Neely) said I had admitted that I had been guilty of an infraction of some law or other. I say that is an absolute untruth-if that language is parliamentary- and he must withdraw it, and withdraw it unconditionally.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The h.on. gentleman for Humboldt (Mr. Neely) certainly made a statement in regard to certain actions of the member for Dauphin; I did not myself hear that the words used were unparliamentary. But if the member for Dauphin denies having done the act attributed to him, by the member for Humboldt, his denial must be accepted.
Well, Mr. Chairman, it is a very strange thing that I am called upon to deny a thing before I have said it.
I again rise to a point of order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I think the hon. member (Mr. Neely) must be allowed to complete his withdrawal. The hon. member made a statement with reference to a certain act by the member for Dauphin, the denial of the member for Dauphin must be accepted. That is the rule of parliament, irrespective of what the hon. member for Humboldt may believe. When
he has once charged an act to the member for Dauphin, which that hon. gentleman denies, it is that parliamentary acceptance of the denial that the member for Humboldt is asked to give.

Well, if the member for Dauphin says he never made the statement on the platform in his constituency in the last Dominion election, that he or his firm spent a certain amount of money in order to obtain the consent of an official of the department to obtain a grazing lease in the west, then of course I will accept the hon. gentleman's statement.
Mr. Chairman, I am quite ready to make the statement at any time, but that is not my point of order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is correct. The particular statement that the member for Humboldt made, not any modification or explanation of it, if the hon. member for Dauphin denies it, that denial under the rules of parliament must be accepted, ft is simply a withdrawal of that particular statement in that form, and not in any other.

I have no recollection of stating anything that the member for Dauphin did until a moment ago. I did not elaborate or make any statement, and the hon. gentleman's denial, and his emphatic language towards myself as to the truth of my statement, were altogether out of order, because I had not stated what the nature of the offence was. It is only the last time I was on my feet that I did so, that I made the explanation. The hon. gentleman cannot deny what I had not said. I made the statement the last time I was on my feet_as to what the particular thing was that I charged the hon. member with. I say again that if the hon. gentleman states that he never made these statements on a public platform, I will take his word for it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has just stated that if the member for Dauphin denies having used the words attributed to him, or the statement, he, the member for Humboldt, accepts that denial.

I am not going to have the onus put on me. I have risen to a point of order. The member for Humboldt stated-I do not know the exact words, but the meaning was that I had admitted having committed some crime for some reason or other. I rose to < that point of order. What object would I have had, if he had not made a statement of that kind, questioning my truthfulness, in rising to a point of order? I surely had some incentive to get on my feet in something that he had said. ^ absolutely insist

on fairplay, I expect to get it, I always do get it. I absolutely insist that the hon. gentlemen take back that statement in the form he made it, that I had admitted having done something that was not within the law, to obtain something for myself or somebody else.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It is somewhat unfortunate that the question has been mixed with other questions, and that the memory of members, as well as of the Chairman, is not as clear as it was at the moment. But the general rule remains, that when a member of this House attributes a certain act to another member which that other member denies, his denial must be accepted. It is now unfortunately too late to recall the exact words; in my memory they appeared to be in this form, that the hon. member for Dauphin had admitted urging the officials of the department to do some act not in the best interests of the country.
That is exactly what I said.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: But I do not recall the word ' illegally ' being used or implied. But even in that form, if the member for Dauphin denies, then the member for Humboldt must, under our parliamentary rules, accept the denial.
I have not withdrawn anything yet.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think that under all the circumstances the expressions of the member for Humboldt would be fairly considered a withdrawal of that statement.

I just want to say this, and say it so that you will understand it, and the House will understand it, and if it gets beyond the confines of the House, that everybody will understand it-I have never in my life made a statement that, by myself, in any way personally, as came out in the ' Free Press ' article that was read by the member for Humboldt, I had bribed, or got any one to bribe, any high official of the Department of the Interior to obtain any concession, whether right or wrong. I want to say emphatically that any one, whether it is the Free Press, or any one else on its behalf, the member for -Humboldt, or any one on his behalf, or on behalf of the Minister of the Interior-I am sorry to drag him into it-says a thing like that about me, he lies, and lies by the clock.
Order.

Well, Mr. Chairman, if my hon. friend denies ever haying made any such statement I accept his denial. I am quite prepared to apply the whitewash brush and put my hon. friend on a pedestal. He tells us that he has never been guilty Mr. CAMPBELL.
of doing anything wrong, and never did any harm.
I beg your pardon, I am not going to be misinterpreted, Mr. Chairman. I rise to a question of privilege.
