speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext:
House again in Committee of the Whole on Bill (No. 93) to incorporate the Alberta Electric Railway Company.-Mr. McCarthy.
On section 14: right to acquire and operate coal mines,

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: I do not see any objection to giving the company these rights. I think the Canadian Pacific railway are operating a coal mine at Bankhead in the Rocky mountains. I do not see any special reason why a railway company should not operate a coal mine or coal mines, because they are the largest consumers of coal.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think my hon. friend is in error, I do not think the Canadian Pacific railway are operating the mines at Bankhead.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is a subsidiary company.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not think the Canadian Pacific railway are operating any coal mines anywhere, neither is the Canadian Northern, although I do not know if they have authority to do so. I wish to repeat most emphatically the objections I offered once before to this Bill. In my judgment the linking together of authority to mine coal and to transport it by rail is detrimental to the best interests of coal mining, and of the consumers of coal who would be affected by this charter. I wish on behalf of the people of Alberta to register a most emphatic protest against the granting of

these powers in this charter. What has been alleged to be a precedent is not a precedent, but if we pass this charter then we will establish a precedent which will no doubt have an injurious effect in the future.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: I was not aware that my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior had expressed an objection to this section. Of course he speaks largely for the section of the country affected, and his views are entitled to very great respect, but it seems to me it is impossible to prevent a railway company from operating a coal mine if it wants - to. What difference does it make whether the Canadian Pacific railway operate a coal mine in their own name, or through another company, the stock of which they have acquired. I understand the Canadian Northern have acquired coal fields at Brazeau, and I do not know that it makes any difference whether they operate those fields in the name of the Canadian Northern or another company. There might be advantages in having another company for financial reasons, for the raising of the money on bonds or stock of that company, but if they control the subsidiary company it is about the same thing as if they were all under the same name.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
That point was under discussion when the Bill was up before, and while no one will pretend that the same men who constitute a railway company may not also constitute a coal company and thereby work in unison to the detriment of the public, the reason this company wants this authority to handle coal incorporated in their charter is in order that the two interests shall be interwoven so that the companies cannot be dealt with separately by controlling legislation. Everybody realizes that there must be controlling legislation as to transportation, and most people recognize that there will have to be controlling legislation in regard to coal mining. If the coal mining interest is legally a separate interest it can be dealt with by controlling legislation very much more conveniently and satisfactorily than if it is united by legislation with the transportation interests. Certain special privileges must be given to transportation companies, or they cannot carry on their business. There is no special privilege required for the carrying on of a coal mining business. But when the coal mining business is put under the same legislative authority, and given the same legislative privileges as a transportation company, then there is a danger that it will escape from future legislative control. That I am satisfied this company is seeking, and it would certainly be to the detriment of the public. It is in the interests of coal mines and of the capital invested in them
that there should be an absolute separation of interest between transportation and coal mining so that the man who owns the coal mine shall get a square deal in the matter of transportation, and it is just as much in the interests of the consumer that there should be actual competition in the producing of coal that the railway company should stand in the position of a common carrier in dealing with the coal mine operator at the one end and the coal consumer at the other. No matter what the private interests of the individuals who constitute a railway company may be, we know that we have the right of legislative control which we can exercise if they are separate legal entities in a manner that we cannot exercise it if they are not separate

I am not positive whether or not the charters obtained by other railway companies give them the right to operate, but it is well known throughout the west that the big companies do own coal mines and I think operate-them to a considerable extent. The Canadian Pacific railway are operating the Hosmer coal mine, although perhaps not very successfully. The Canadian Northern railway have acquired coa. rights all along the foot-hills in fact, between my town and Calgary, and I think the Grand Trunk Pacific have been purchasing or acquiring coal mining rights, although I am not positive about that. The Minister of Railways the other evening said that in the near future parliament would have to interfere with those companies, and take from them the rights they have acquired under their charters to operate coal mines. For that reason I take it for granted that they all have these rights in their charters. In that case I do not see why we should start now to make a precedent in the case of this company and take away the rights they are asking for, and not give them a fair chance to be on a level with other railway companies oper-pating in the western country. That is all I have to say and I do not think there is any more to be said. Other companies have this right, and I do not see why this company should not be put on an equality with the others. It would be a great accommodation to the people if this right were conferred on this company which may serve portions of the country where other larger railroads are not likely to go.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: I would like to know if this were agreed to in the Railway Committee, because if so it would influence me very much.

I am instructed by the Minister of Railways that this section was agreed to as a compromse. There was a clause in the Bill allowing the railway to operate a telephone company, but that was

objected by the province of Alberta, and an arrangement was made between the province and the promoters of the Bill by which the railway company relinquished its right to the telephone clause which had been passed by^ the Railway Committee, and in consideration thereof the province of Alberta agreed that this section should be allowed in the Bill. A distinct arrangement was, therefore, made, and if this clause is^ stricken out then the railway company will have nothing in return for its abandonment of the right to operate telephones. It is pretty well understood that in matters appertaining to their particular departments the ministers in charge are supposed to know more than others and their opinion carries weight. The Minister of the Interior is assumed prima facie to know more about a matter pertaining to his department than would the Minister of Public Works, and the Minister of Railways is supposed to know more about a railway matter than would the Minister of the Interior, and in connection with this principle I quote what the Minister of Railways said this day week, ' Hansard ' 5181:

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
I think we had better let it pass. It was explained in the committee pietty fully. In the west the railway companies practically all own coal areas, and operate them in connection with their traffic. It may be that in the years to come we shall have to cancel all these rights by legislation if they are abused. If it should happen that the coal companies and the transportation companies should put their heads together so that where you reduce the freight rates they will add them to the price of coal, it might be necessary to pass legislation in Canada similar to what has been passed in the United States, prohibiting coal companies and railway companies from being one and the same people.
We, therefore, have the authority of the Minister of Railways that in his judgment this is a proper clause to pass, he being at the time perfectly aware of the arrangement made between the parties.

My recollection is that when the Bill left the Railway Committee it contained the telephone clause, but that the coal clause had been stricken out in the committee. It was discussed to a certain extent in the Railway Committee, and on a vote being taken the telephone clause was left in, and the coal clause rejected. I cannot understand how the Bill gets to this House in its present shape, and in the absence of so many members from Alberta who are interested in the matter it seems to me that the Bill should go back to the Railway Committee for investigation. It is a most remarkable thing that everything we did in the Railway Committee seems to be reversed. In the absence of further light I am still .of opinion that the telephone clause should remain, because I do Mr. NORTHRTTP.
not believe in a monopoly in telephones, and as to the coal matter on general principles I would be opposed to it.
Mr. Chairman, is there a clause (j) added to section 7 in the reprint ?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: There is a paragraph (j) subparagraph of clause 7.

My recollection is that when this Bill left the Railway Committee it contained the telephone clause, and did not contain the coal clause, and I do not understand how it now comes before us in its present shape. I am informed that subsequently there was an arrangement for an exchange of clauses, but I would like to be satisfied as to whether the matter came up again before the Railway Committee, and whether it endorsed that arrangement?

This day week the Bill was in the committee, and I quote from ' Hansard ' page 5179:
On section 12,
I move that section 12 be stricken from the Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
Does Mr. McCarthy agree to that ?
' Mr. DOUGLAS. Yes.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

That refers to the proceedings of the Committee of the Whole House, but I have been referring to the Railway Committee. Whatever arrangement was made it appears to have been made after the Bill left the Railway Committee and under these circumstances it is proper that the Bill should go back to the Railway Committee. We are creating precedents and these precedents should be carefully considered by the Railway Committee which is responsible for railway legislation.
I do not understand the argument that when the Committee of the Whole House has approved of a clause you have to send it upstairs to a standing committee to get that approval confirmed.
I do not understand that the Committee of the Whole House passed on this.
Yes, this day week.

The Committee of the Whole House ordered that the Bill was to stand over for reconsideration, and that is why we are reconsidering it to-night. In the Railway Committee we inserted the telephone clause and struck out the mining clause, but there appears to have been an arrangement made afterwards between the representatives of the province of Alberta, and the promoters of the Bill to transpose the clauses, and that is what the hon.

member (Mr. Northrup) refers to when he reads from ' Hansard ' what was done in this committee the other night. I stated then that I did not like the legislation, but that I was a long distance away from where the road was going to be built, and when the parties agreed 1 did not see any reason why I should dissent. At the same time 1 am opposed to the legislation, and would prefer that this Bill went back to the Railway Committee. If the Railway Committee should agree, I personally would not object to it going through, but I think it ought to be reconsidered by that committee.

In the Committee of the Whole House the Bill was agreed to as it now stands. Why should we send it back to the Railway Committee, which is only a portion of the House, for approval, when the whole House agreed to it?

For the very simple reason that this is a very material change, and that the Railway Committee did not consider it. This change was not proposed by the province of Alberta. That province did not propose to insert the coal clause an# strike out the telephone clause when the Bill was before the Railway Committee. It is only because the Railway Committee did not have the opportunity to consider the Bill in the shape in which it now is, that I ask that it be sent back to them.

With regard to what the hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker) has said, this House has not yet disposed of the matter. The reason we have a Railway Committee is to have these things considered at greater length than they are likely to be considered in this House. The Railway Committee ought to have before it any arrangement made between the representatives of Alberta and the promoters of the Bill. We will only be doing justice to the promoters of the Bill if we send it back. If there were a majority in this House in favour of striking out this coal clause, the reverse of the arrangement which had been arrived at between the promoters and the representatives of Alberta, those who want to see the coal clause in, would still think that the Bill should go back to the Railway Committee.
I think that the Railway Committee is the proper body to discuss these matters before they come into this House.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
What is remarkable in connection with this Bill is that it comes from the Railway Committee in a certain form and then is altered in the Committee of the Whole House in the absence of the promoters. I want to urge upon my hon. friend that this is a matter of too serious importance to be dealt with in that way. It. should be dealt with on the responsibility of those whose business it is to take the evidence and ascertain what merit
there is in favour of this measure. That is the business of the Railway Committee. If that committee should see fit to insert this clause I would waive any objection, but I do not think it is fair to the country or the House that an attempt should be made to have a clause inserted in the Committee of the Whole House after the Railway Committee have struck it out. This has been alluded to as a compromise. A compromise on what? The railway company ask for telephone privileges and a coal mining right. Is it a compromise that they he allowed a coal right instead of a telephone right? What is there to show that they should have either right?
Other companies have the same right.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Other companies have not the same right, so far as my knowledge goes, or ought not to have been given that right if they have it.
I was present in the Railway Committee the other day when a similar Bill, proposed by an hon. member on your right, Mr. Speaker, had a similar clause in it, and that clause was passed.
What Bill was that?
It was a Bill proposed by the hon. member for Brant, and had coal rights in connection with a coal mine in the United States.

I opposed that very Bill in the committee, but it was voted on and
carried.
That is right. You are just confirming what I said.
I want to give the true state of affairs in connection with that Bill. That company was not authorized to mine coal or enter into the business of a coal mining company.
Yes, it was.
It was simply for the purpose of producing coal and distributing it.
What is the difference?

The reason given by the promoters of the Bill was that they were connected with a steamship line across Lake Erie, and the only way they could make the road a success was to operate the road in conjunction with that steamship line, and it could not be operated successfully unless the company had the right to produce the coal and distribute and sell it. That was a very different proposition from giving a railway company the right to mine coal and go into a general business.

657f>
The Lehigh Valley and various companies were mentioned and discussed and the distinction drawn between the Bill referred to by the hon. member for North Ontario (Mr. Sharpe) and the American companies. This Bill seeks to place this company in the same position as the Lehigh and other big American companies. It gives the right to the company to do the business of transportation and coal mining as well. That is quite different from the matter mentioned by the hon. member for North Ontario. Again the question was raised in the Railway Committee that they might create a monopoly by giving this company the right to purchase, sell and distribute coal, but it was proven to the committee that all the territory which would be covered by this proposed railway was now covered by three other railways. The railway mentioned by my hon. friend was an electric road, and the cases are not all analogous.

There is no objection to this railway going into the coal mining business if it does it through a subsidiary company. That is the way other companies are doing, but you put a clause in allowing this company, which is not a steam railway company but an electric railway company, to enable it to go into the coal mining business. The main object of a clause is for promoting purposes, and the arrangement made in the way of a compromise, as I understand the matter, was not made by the Railway Committee, but by the Committee of the Whole House and between two or three members of the House. For my part I am opposed to either clause. I am opposed to giving this railway company the right to go into the telephone business in Alberta. The government of that province own the telephone business, which they purchased; and they do not want other companies to go into that same business. Just the same in the coal mining business.
A great deal of disadvantage may, and does, come to other miners of coal who have not a railway. Put this company on exactly the same footing as other coal miners. They will still have the advantage of having the railway, if they care to take the necessary steps, to go into the coal mining business. To that we can take no exception. But I do take most strenuous exception to any more railway companies being allowed to compete with the coal mine owners who have not equal privileges. This is a most unreasonable clause, and I do not see why its removal should be objected to. These parties can, if they wish, secure a charter, either from the local government or under the Dominion Companies Act, giving them all the powers they want for mining coal, but let that coal mining charter be separate from the railway charter, especially seeing that Mr. CARVELL.
this is to be an electric railway and is not supposed to be going into the coal hauling business.
Mr. OLIVER, I have agreed with my hon. friend (Mr. Turriff), with regard to the attitude taken on this Bill, but I have to disagree with him on one point lie mentions-that this company was not incorporated to go into the coal business. I had not the advantage of reading the charter before, but I find that it is certainly a very remarkable one-it is a blanket charter, covering the whole of the coal bearing area of southern Alberta. If ever there was a charter brought into this House with the deliberate intention of creating a monopoly in the mining and transportation of coal, this is that charter. The works of the company are set out in nine separate divisions.
(a)	From a point at or near the city of Calgary to the town of Banff in the Rocky Mountain Park.
(b)	From a point at or near the said city of Calgary south of the Bow river, through or near the Thigh Falls, to the city of Medicine Hat. crossing the Bow river at a point between Little Rolling Hills and Grand Forks.
All coal lands

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, all coal lands.
(c)	From the said railway between Calgary and Medicine Hat, at a point in or near Long Cculee, to the city of Lethbridge.
Everybody knows whether Lethbridge is a coal mining centre or not.
(d)	From a point on the said railway between Calgary and Medicine Hat at or near Expanse Coulee to the town of Taber, thence westerly to the city of Lethbridge, thepce to the said railway between Calgary and Medicine Hat, at a point on the said railway at or near Long Coulee.
That is the route of the railway.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, that is the route of the railway. If it has any purpose, it is to gather the coal area of southern Alberta into one merger under colour of a railway charter.
Could not they do that under a separate charter?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Not to the same advantage..
(e)	From a point on the said railway between Calgary and Medicine Hat, at or near the Thigh Hills, to the town of Macleod.
(f)	From a point at or near the city of Calgary to the town of Carbon and thence to the Red Deer river at or near the junction of the Knee Hill, creek.
Another coal area.
(g)	From a point at or near the city of Lethbridge to the international boundary line at or near the point where the south branch

of the Milk river crosses the said international boundary line.
(h)	From the city of Medicine Hat to the town of Wood Mountain, in the province of Saskatchewan.
(i)	From a point at or near the city of Calgary to the town of Brooks, passing through or near Windermere, Strathmore and Bassano, with power to construct branch lines from the said lines of railway in the districts known as the Canadian Pacific irrigation blocks.
I cannot prophesy what would be the result of the passing of this, charter but the Bill carries its purpose on its face, and that purpose undoubtedly is to create a monopoly in the production and transportation of coal in the whole of southern Alberta. They apply to this parliament for a charter to build these lines, which, if they were built, and not under any special privilege, would, of course, be of advantage in the development of the coal mining industry. But when to the privileges of a railway company are added the privilege of conducting a coal mining business in that country, anybody can see what advantage there is to the mine that is connected with this proposed octopus railway as compared with a mine not connected with that railway. It simply puts the men who own the transportation and a few mines in a position to put the other miners out of business. Mr. Chairman, this is a most serious consideration. When I heard the matter brought up first, I thought it was possibly a mere accident that the clause regarding the mining of coal was inserted in the Bill, but, on careful consideration of the Bill, I must say I consider this measure an attack on the welfare of the southern part of Alberta, and, that being my view. I feel bound to confess that while, if that provision were withdrawn, I would say it was a meritorious enterprise, yet, so long as that provision remains in the Bill I wrould say it is entitled to all the opposition that any friend of Southern Alberta can give it.

How about the Galt Co.? They have been operating coal mines from the earliest days of that country and operating a railway also, yet I have heard no objection. I have not their charter under nry hand, but I have always understood it was both a steam railway and a coal charter. What is the difference between a railway company owning a coal .mine, and a coal mine company owning a railway? We have been been putting through railway charters-doing it right along- in the part of the country in which I live.

The Galt railway was chartered many years ago. It was the first railway, outside of the Canadian Pacific railway, to operate in that country, and the first company in western Canada to
operate a coal mine. They have done very good work in the past, and they are doing good work now.
And there have never been any complaints.

I have never heard any complaints about them. But they are in a different position there from the coal mining companies in the Crowsnest Pass, for instance. I may say also that I understand, the Galt Railway Company have sold out their railway, so that they have now only the coal mine as a separate work from the railway. Last year, I heard complaints from a mine owner and operator in the Crowsnest Pass. He pointed out that one of the mines was connected with one of the large railway companies, and that mine could always get the large, open, steel cars to load their coal, while the other mines had to take the box cars. That is not a very big matter, but it may easily mean 10, 15 or 20 cents of an addition on every ton of coal shipped, which is a profit in itself. Not only thsC but if the railway company is interested in a coal mine, I do not care how the commission tries to prevent it, the railway company and their officials are bound to give the advantage to the mine in which they are interested. That is all we want to obviate. Let this company have their coal mining rights, but let it be a separate and distinct company; and if we have done wrong in the past many years ago by authorizing some company to operate railways and coal mines, the time has come when we should do it no longer, and the time will come shortly when those railway companies that now operate coal mines will have to be dealt with separately, and the interest will have to be separated. In the meantime there is no reason why we should allow this company which professes to be mainly an electric railway company, the right to operate a coal mine.
Deal with them all alike. The minister suggested that the other evening, and I agree to that.

So far as I am concerned, they all will be dealt with alike in the future. I will never support again a railway charter, in this House or any other house, that carries with it the right to operate a coal mine. Take another point in this Bill. The capitalization for the enterprise is $10,000,000. This company might very easily utilize the half of that capital, or all of it, in coal mining enterprises. that would be easy to accomplish under this charter. So there is no good reason advanced, except that it has been done in the past, why the House should authorize this company to acquire and operate coal mines; and I hope the good

sense of the company will see that that clause is not allowed to remain in the Bill.

There is another consideration I would like to see discussed by this committee. I would prefer hearing the discussion carried on in the Railway Committee, but as the Bill is not being referred there, probably we have to discuss these matters in the House.
Is the hon. gentleman opposed to the clause?
I will be obliged to oppose it unless it is referred back to the Railway Committee.
And what then?

Then I will probably oppose it. We are in the habit of granting railway companies other powers than those merely of building and operating a railway, powers, for instance, with regard to the acquisition of water-powers, the building of telegraph and telephone lines, all those powers which are used incidentally by a railway company. Here we have the right given to a railway company to mine coal, a purpose that is not in any sense incidental to or necessary in a carrying company. The point that strikes me is this, that if we give this company the right to mine coal, it has a right to carry its own coal as free as it has to carry gravel, that is necessary on its own road, or its necessary iron, or anything else. Some time there may be an application before the Railway Commission to fix the rates for carrying coal from one point to another. The coal which is mined and owned by this company will be carried free, the cost of carrying must be paid by some person, and I submit to this House that it is altogether likely that the cost of carrying coal belonging to this company will be put over on other coal companies, because coal must pay the cost of its carriage. If this company is allowed to mine coal and to carry its own coal, the Railway Commission may not require any separate account to be kept of the carrying charges of this company's coal, and there will be difficulty in properly apportioning the rates of carrying coal from one point to another, and as between other coal companies and this railway company.
Did not the hon. gentleman support an identical clause in the Bill presented by the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Harris) in the Railway Committee the other day?

I do not remember having expressed myself one way or the other, but as I was in the Railway Committee at that time, I am ready to take the responsibility of saying that I did support it. I have no recollection of it to-day. I remember some discussion about it, and Mr. TURRIFF.
for reasons which were given to the Railway Committee at that time, and which were considered by them as sufficient, the thing went through.
How does the hon. gentleman reconcile that with his present position?
The special circumstances, which I need not go into here, were considered by the committee, and were not the same as we find in this Bill.

I happen to have the Bill under my hand to which I referred in my question, Bill (No. 106), clause 11. The clause gives the company power, for the purposes of its undertaking of buying, selling and dealing in coal or lumber, and other commodities.

If my hon. friend's memory was half as good as it ought to be, he would know, and he does know, that lumber and other commodities were cut out of the Bill; and the hon. gentleman is not quoting the section that passed the Railway Committee, and he knows it.

If the hon. gentleman will have patience, I will tell him that the passage in the section referring to coal and iron was maintained in the clause, and it was on my own motion that lumber and other commodities were struck out, and the reference to coal and ore still remains in the charter. Now I simply rose to emphasize the inconsistency of the hon. gentlemen who oppose this clause in this Bill. It seems an extraordinary circumstance that if the Bill is proposed by an hon. member on the government side, it may contain a clause that is broad enough to include the purchasing and selling of coal, and which would be detrimental to the public interest, according to the arguments advanced by the member for Saskatoon; but because it is proposed by another hon. member of this House, it meets with his disapprobation.
Mr. Mc-CRANEY. I hope my hon, friend is not suggesting that because the one Bill was proposed by a member on this side of the House, and the present Bill was proposed by an hon. member of the opposition, that that fact changes my point of view.

I asked the hon. gentleman how he reconciles his present position with his conduct the other day, and I cannot account for it on any other ground. The clause in the Bill having for its sponsor, the hon. membelr for Brantford, is broad enough to include the purchase of coal mines and selling or dealing in coal, another clause gives the right of selling and dealing in coal or ore. That is comprehensive enough to include coal mines, the company could purchase coal mines and deal

in coal mines; if they can purchase coal, they can purchase coal mines. Consequently, it would be very entertaining and would be a matter of information to the House if the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Mc-Craney) would explain and reconcile his two positions.
I would like very much indeed to do it before the Railway Committee, but I am afraid there is not time now in two minutes to do it here.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: What section is my hon. friend quoting from?
The hon. member for Carleton, New Brunswick (Mr. Car-veil), has it before him.
No, you had better state it; I cannot find it here.
Section 111.
What Bill?

Bill (No. 106).
were cases in which men had transgressed the law and had not been prosecuted.
That is the fact, die said that there are cases in which men have transgressed and have been prosecuted, that in some cases men's entries have been cancelled, and they have been given no consideration, and in other cases men have been allowed to purchase at a price. Each case rests upon its individual merits. We cannot pretend to deal with all the cases alike, because if we did that, it would not be the fair way to deal with them, the merits being different under different circumstances. I had the opportunity of making inquiry regarding the cases of which my hon. friend spoke in the interval between six and eight o'clock, and I think the committee will agree with me that these are flagrant cases. One of them is the case of J. A. Cathers. This gentleman had three homesteads, and he has been sentenced, not by the Department of the Interior
In what province?
Oh, I beg your pardon.

speechtext: What time is it now?
In so far as I am concerned I am not subject to the accusation that I was inconsistent. I would like to point out to my hon. friend that the two Bills are different.
It is only the difference between buying coal and dealing in coal.

Of course, the hon. member for North Ontario says that 'dealing' means that they cannot buy a coal mine as well as coal mined. Probably he is right. I would not like to dispute that. This road was running through the southern part of Ontario where every little town and village is served with railways that have as good connections as they could get with coal mines.

speechtext: When the committee rose at six o'clock, if the discussion then proceeding has ceased, there was some consideration of certain cases in which persons who had transgressed the law were suffering the penalty. I do not wish to enlarge on this particular side of the question more than to say that in so far as I am aware, and in so far as the intent of the department is concerned, we wish to deal even-handed justice between man and man. We do not want to give one man different treatment from another man. The hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Campbell) said that there 176

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I could not say what province they were in, but the last ease, that which got him into trouble, occurred in Saskatchewan. It was not in Manitoba, and was not in the constituency of the hon. member for Dauphin. John Boyd had four homesteads, and Sam Boyd had two homesteads. Another of the family, William Boyd, had four homesteads, and I understand that proceedings are now pending against him. I cannot give any information as to the details of these cases at the moment. Of course, the papers could easily be brought before the House on an order, but I think the committee will agree with me that when a man has secured his fourth homestead he is not in a position to claim very favourable consideration. He is not in the position of the man who has had one homestead, and who might in some way or another have erred as to his rights with regard to a second. I think it is fair to assume that the cases in regard to which the discussion took place were exceedingly flagrant, and it would not have been fair to the law-abiding citizen, the law-abiding settler who wanted a homestead to have overlooked such flagrant cases. In the present condition of the country where there is a demand for land, and where honest men are honestly trying to get the best homesteads they can, it is not fair to them to allow a man who is not entitled to a homestead to get one, or, if he gets one unfairly, to retain it.
Mr. Chairman, I,do not know the particulars with regard to all these cases. I believe that Cathers, the man spoken of first by the minister, had perfect liberty under the law to take two homesteads.

May I call attention to a case in which there appears to have been discrimination. I brought the case to the attention of the minister in 1907. An order in council is published granting a homestead on payment of $5 an acre to the man whose case I called to the attention of the minister. This man homesteaded in 1902. In 1907 charges were made that he had not been four days on his homestead during the whole time. It was charged that this was his third homestead, and I read to the House a letter in which that charge was made. I subsequently sent a similar letter to the Department of the Interior. There were many applicants for that homestead. The minister decided that cancellation should not take place and cancellation apparently did not take place. The Minister of the Interior submits, under date the 28th September, 1910, that Mr. John Bradley made homestead entry for the northwest I of section 36, township 21, range 8, west of the 2nd meridian on the 30th October, 1902, and has made application for patent.

It will be observed that the order in council does not say that Mr. Bradley has performed his necessary duties, it simply calls attention to the improvements which he has put upon the land and is entirely silent in regard to the residence. Therefore, we may take it for granted that the duties have not been done and he has not performed the necessary residence duties, although I have always understood from the minister that the residence duties rank first of all, and that except in the most exceptional cases they are never allowed to be waived. I have seen other orders in council in respect of men who had already exhausted their right of homestead, who had got illegal entries to homesteads, but in these cases it has generally been stated that the minister is satisfied that the second entry was made through ignorance or some such reason as that. In Mr. Bradley's ease that is not stated. In all other cases I have noticed it has been stated that all the residence and other duties have been carried out, so we now have one particular case in which illegal entry was made, and in which the minister in his order in council does not even claim that the illegal entry was made in ignorance or by mistake; yet without the fulfilment of the necessary duties that man is given a patent for his land on payment of $5 per acre. It seems to me that is quite as bad a case as the others to which reference has been made, and it would appear as if there had been discrimination in this case. I shall not charge that until I have healrd what the minister has to say in respect of
It.

I can assure my hon. friend that as he has called attention to this case I shall take more care in future that such a thing shall not occur again. I shall take the best care I can to prevent it, because I feel that the very foundation of our success-and I think the House will admit that we have won some measure of success in settling that western country-is that there be a feeling of confidence in the fair dealing of the department as between man and man. No harder blow could be struck at the success of our settlement policy than the suggestion that one man is treated differently from another.

brought it to the attention of the House at least twice, and I think three times.

speechtext: This government has no responsibility for sending any man to jail.

speechtext: In other cases the department thought it was necessary to prosecute and did prosecute. In this case they have known for years that Bradley committed perjury and instead of prosecuting him they have rewarded him by giving him the land at a great deal less than its value. I have not in my mind the very case referred to, but I presume that in the opinion of the department the cases were not similar. speechtext: Mr.. OLIVER. We have nothing whatever to* do with the criminal law and are not bound to enforce it in any way. Any one who thinks that the criminal law has been violated by this man is at liberty to set in motion the machinery of justice and let justice take its course.

subtopic: HIS EXCELLENCY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL IN COUNCIL.
speechtext: I do not like to be on my feet so often and appear so pertinacious, but I would like to know why, when the minister has the evidence in his department that this man Bradley, as is affirmed by my hon. friend from Qu Appelle (Mr. Lake) to-night, took at least three homesteads some four or five years ago, and did not conform with the law in any particular at all as far as residence goes, and perjured himself in making the entries-I would like to know why this man has been protected by the officers of the Interior Department and not prosecuted. Instead he gets a presentation of three-quarters of that land and gets for $600 or $800 a homestead worth $2,400 or $2,500. If the minister will say that he will inquire fully^ into this matter and prosecute this man, if he finds the allegations against him to be true, I have nothing more to say. But if the minister is not going to do that, I shall have a great deal more to say.

cases.

If it belongs there why is it .not left there in every case? What I do not understand is why the Min-

ister of the Interior or the Department of Justice found it necessary to prosecute some of these men and put them in jail, and not prosecute others, but leave their cases to be dealt with by the province. Why not deal with every case or with none?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: HIS EXCELLENCY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL IN COUNCIL.
speechtext: I do not know that I can give any further explanation. The cases differ in degree and we deal with each on its merits, and we do not pretend to be infallible. To suggest that we should deal with all cases in exactly the same way is not a wise suggestion.

subtopic: HIS EXCELLENCY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL IN COUNCIL.
speechtext: I do not say that, hut all these parties have perjured themselves, as I understand.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: HIS EXCELLENCY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL IN COUNCIL.
speechtext:
There may be extenuating circumstances in one case and not in another. The hon. member for Dauphin has been pleading extenuating circumstances in the cases of men who have been convicted, and. there might be such circumstances in other cases. No doubt we commit errors, but the policv of the department is to treat all men equally and give each man what is coming to him as we understand it. It is certainly not our policy to treat men differently because of their political opinion. When I was a private member I had a great deal of business with the Interior Department on behalf of my constituency, and I never was asked what were the political views of the men for whom I was acting. I never asked the question myself of any of my constituents, nor did the department ever ask me the question. Since I have had charge of the department, my instructions to the officials have always been to deal with every man according to the merits of his case without regard to his political views. That is one of the reasons why there has been a very considerable measure of success with the administration of the department. It is because the people feel that they are getting a square deal.
Now, if I may be permitted, I wish to say a word to my hon. Mends on my right who criticise the actions of the department from the opposite point of view from that of my hon. friends on the other side. The same principle applies exactly. We want to create the impression in the public mind of absolute fairplay between man and man in all the dealings of the department. Those who were members of the House when the Bill of 1908 was introduced will remember that the late Hon. Thomas Greenway, who was a member of the House at that time, criticised the Bill quite severely because it was, as he said, 'too wooden' in its operation;-that is, it did not leave enough discretion to the department to administer the law so as to meet all the variety of eases that can arise. His criticism was
perfectly sound and had very good foundation. But he was dealing with conditions as he had known them in years gone by, and condtions had changed. The Bill of 1908 was framed to deal with conditions as they then were-and, even mbre especially, as they were going to be. When there were two or three thousand homestead entries in a year, it was possible for attention to be given to individual cases, and for all the cases to be carried, as might be said, in the heads of the officers of the department and full consideration to be given according to the actual merits of each case. But with thirty, and forty, and fifty, and sixty, and seventy thousand entries a year, that kind of treatment becomes an absolute impossibility. Under such conditions, a rule must be laid down, and that rule must be followed; otherwise, there can Be but one result-confusion and dissatisfaction. Now, it must be admitted that in laying down a rule, you do work hardship in some cases. But my view is that, if we work hardship in some cases-and we alleviate hardship as much as we can-the main point we are striving for is to create confidence in the public mind that there is a square deal for every man in the transactions of the department. And the results show that we have attained it in a very remarkable degree. It is not con ceivable that the occupation of the land would have gone on as rapidly as it has during the past year or two if the people had not had full confidence that they were being dealt with on the merits of their application, and without regard to any other consideration whatever. I think it is one of the greatest tributes that could have been paid to the administration of any government that, when, from time to time, we opened for occupation, townships here or there throughout the west, people came by the trainload from the United States and from various parts of Canada in order to take their places in the line to secure their turn in entering for that land. Men stood in line for twenty-four hours, for forty-eight hours,-some, I believe, for seventy hours-
Mr. SOHAFFNER Women, too.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: HIS EXCELLENCY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL IN COUNCIL.
speechtext: Women, too,-in order to get their choice of the land. They wouid not have done that if they had not thought at anyrate that when they got to the counter they would get a square deal. I think that the actual facts have justified the administration of the department to a most remarkable degree. While we have not been able to meet all possible cases that arose upon their actual merits, we have certainly been able to create in the public mind that confidence which is the very foundation of all success in administration.

subtopic: HIS EXCELLENCY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL IN COUNCIL.
speechtext:
The Minister (Mr. Oliver) has just told you and this com-

mittee, Mr. Chairman, that his prime desire has been to create the impression in the minds of the people that fairplay is his object. He has gone on to point out that at various land agencies, as land was thrown open, the crowd stood for hours with a desire to have the pick of the land, and that every one who took his position was allowed to pass through the doorway in -his turn, and, at the counter, got fairplay. There is no one on this side who would criticise that for a moment. The government, possibly, could not, even if they desired, under the present law and in the open, do otherwise than give entry to every man in his turn. We are not criticising that point. The point we are criticising is that, when the time comes for these people to apply for their patents, the same fairplay is not given by the officials of the department to one as to another. The hon. minister has expressed regret that such things had occurred as were brought to his attention by my hon. friend from Qu'Appelle (Mr. Lake). I will tell the minister how he could remove from the public mind a great deal of the fear that such things can exist. If he were to cleanse his department in the west to some degree; if he would remember that the Conservatives of the west have a suspicion-or a superstition or whatever he likes to call it; it is stronger than either, it is a conviction -about certain appointees of his government that they are not inclined to show fairplay to those tainted with Conservatism, he would do something to realize the wish he has expressed. I refer to such men as Mr. Seale, one of his homestead inspectors-(I do not know that 'Inspectors' is the proper word, but the minister will know what I want to get at). Why did Mr. Seale get that appointment? For no other reason on earth that any Tory in the west can elucidate except that in 1904 he was the returning officer for Dauphin, and, at the eleventh hour he made the Dauphin election a postponed election. Immediately after that he got the appointment at $100 a month from the government. He-never served the government in his life except in the way I am suggesting, and in that he was serving only a part of the people and not the people as a whole. Then, go further west, and right in the home town, I think, of my hon. friend from Humboldt (Mr. Neely) is Mr. Duggan.

subtopic: HIS EXCELLENCY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL IN COUNCIL.
speechtext: A good man, too.

subtopic: HIS EXCELLENCY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL IN COUNCIL.
speechtext: A handy man.
