speechtext:
I am not saying anything against Mr. Duggan personally, except that my hon. friend from Macdonald (Mr. Staples) says he was a very handy man. He was the returning officer for Selkirk at 1904. He had never served under the government in his life. He had been previously to that a bartender in Selkirk. He served under Leach, in what is called Mr. CAMPBELL.
among the Conservatives of Manitoba the Thin Red Line outrage, where hundreds of Conservatives were debarred from voting, and their franchise was stolen from them; and the Conservatives believe that was the reason he got employment under this government. I could go on and instance other cases. But this is what I want to point out to the minister, that if he wishes the people on both sides of politics in the west to believe in his good faith-as perhaps we all do, in his personal good faith-but I mean in the good faith of his department in its administration of the land laws, the sooner he gets rid of these excresences, the better for the country.

subtopic: HIS EXCELLENCY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL IN COUNCIL.
speechtext:
In reference to the remarks of the Minister of the Interior as to ^complaints made by myself and others in 'regard to the administration of the lands, I only want to say that I for one have never suggested for a moment that- there was any discrimination between man and man on the part of the minister or of the department, because I do not think there is, I never knew of any, at all events. But what I have maintained before the minister himself on many occasions is that while you may be giving all hands the same deal, that deal may be a hard one, and unnecessarily hard. In my judgment there are many cases where leniency could be shown to a settler that is not shown, and that makes it harder for him. Where you have 60,000 or
70,000	homesteaders in a year, forty-nine out of fifty of them go there for the purpose of making a home, for the purpose of fulfilling the conditions. Out of so large a number there are many who find it difficult to fulfil all the conditions ot the law at the present time. Owing to the tremendous demand for land, they are forced to go away forty or fifty miles from a railway to make an entry. They go out there with a small means, and travel long distances, they have to haul their goods, their coal and provisions forty or fifty miles, may be, then a prairie fire burns up all the field. They may not be able to spend the winter there, and have to go on further. In many cases a man goes to make a homestead entry, he has a wife and children, and in my judgment great leniency should be shown to him. Where circumstances warrant it, an extension of time should be granted for going on their lands. That is not going to hurt anybody, cannot hurt anybody. In my constituency there are cases where I have applied for these little extensions of time, and for other considerations of one kind or another, many that the minister himself never sees, and the.officers write me that they regret that under the regulations of the department it is impossible to grant the request. Now I do not claim that there is discrimination, I know there is not, but I

claim that some consideration might be shown with advantage to the settlers. The object of the Homestead Act is to settle up the country, we want settlers, and we want to keep them there. But there is many a good man who finds himself in a difficult situation because, especially of late years, there is a percentage of men who make homestead entries, and who are not bona tide homesteaders', and on their account bona fide homesteaders, who are at a disadvantage as to means perhaps, have to go further and have to suffer. I think the minister could well show greater leniency in many cases to the settlers than he does now, and nobody would be hurt, and nobody would have a right to complain.

subtopic: HIS EXCELLENCY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL IN COUNCIL.
speechtext:
I agree with the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Turriff) that a good deal of leniency should be shown to the homesteader in western Canada. I sympathize with him as fully as any person, because I took up a homestead in western Canada in the early days, and went through all the hardships. Now here we have two cases. One is that of a man named Carrutliers, who went to work and took up two homesteads. He was entitled to these two homesteads, but he went a little further and he took up a third homestead, and he took a false affidavit in order to get this third homestead. I am told by my hon. friend from Dauphin who knows the man very well, that he is a good Tory. The department finds out that this man is a good Tory, they also find out that he has done something wrong, and they go alter him and send him to jail for a year or two. My hon. friend from Saskatchewan tells us of another case under the very same circumstances. He is entitled to two homesteads, and he goes to work and takes one more homestead that he is not entitled to. This man turns out to be a good Reformer, and the department allows that man-I do not say it is because he is a Reformer, but it looks a good deal like it-allows that man to buy his homestead for $5 an acre, and he does not have to go to jail. Now the hon. minister told us that in many cases where they got mixed up in their homesteads some were charged $2, some $3, some $4, some $5 and some $6. I would like to know according to what standard the minister charges $2 to a man who should pay $3, $4 or $5 for those lands. He also says that he has no Tight to prosecute these men. I think if there is any man in Canada who is responsible for the land of this country it is the Minister of the Interior. If Canada is being robbed of her land, if it is not the minister's duty to go after the people who are robbing Canada, I would like to know whose duty it is. I would like the minister to tell us by what standard he
charges one man only $3 and another $4 or $5 for the same land.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: HIS EXCELLENCY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL IN COUNCIL.
speechtext: It would be hard to make a general statement that would cover the questions my hon. friend has asked. If he mentions an individual case I would be able to give the reasons by which we arrived at our conclusion in regard to that case. But to give him any general statement that would be a definite guide to the conclusions we have reached in cases which differ so tremendously in character, would be a very difficult thing to do.

subtopic: HIS EXCELLENCY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL IN COUNCIL.
speechtext: In what way will they differ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: HIS EXCELLENCY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL IN COUNCIL.
speechtext: There are some cases where a boy takes land and he is under age, there are some cases where a man has done a great deal of improvement, another man has done residence and not much improvement, there is another case where the department may have had reasonable grounds for believing that the man acted in ignorance; there are nearly as many differences as there are cases. In these circumstances I do not think I can give my hon. friend any very full details. He wras in error in one thing. We do not sell at $3 per acre unless in cases outside of the preempted area, for the reason that I have already stated. Within the pre-emption area the standard price is $3. Therefore, in settling such a case outside of the area we must reasonably charge more than $3; otherwise it will be practically extending the pre-emption area over the whole country.

subtopic: HIS EXCELLENCY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL IN COUNCIL.
speechtext: The reason I mentioned $3 was that the minister had spoken of $3 before six o'ciock.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: HIS EXCELLENCY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL IN COUNCIL.
speechtext: Yes, but that is inside of the pre-emption area, but in cases outside of the pre-emption area we naturally have to charge more.

subtopic: HIS EXCELLENCY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL IN COUNCIL.
speechtext: I see that outside of the preemption area a man named Charles R. Dux-bury was given his land at $3 an acre, the statement being that he had failed to perform his residence duties. There the minister recommends a sale at $3 an acre.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: HIS EXCELLENCY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL IN COUNCIL.
speechtext:
That is not the same case as that in which a man has committed perjury in order to get a homestead. I might explain to the committee that there are cases where a man has fulfilled in a reasonable measure his obligations as to residence and cultivation, but for some reason which seems to the department to be sufficient, is not able to complete his residence so as to entitle him to the patent. The committee is aware that we cannot issue a patent unless and until the man is able to swear, and to bring two other witnesses to swear, that he has completed his duties in every

particular. If a man is short of his residence and the circumstances are such that it is not possible or practicable to complete his residence and he stands in danger of losing the time he put in and the improvements he has done on his land, we cancel his entry and sell him the land, and in some cases we sell it to him at one dollar per acre.

subtopic: HIS EXCELLENCY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL IN COUNCIL.
speechtext: The reason for his failure to perform the residence should be stated in the order in council. It generally is in these cases, is it not?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: HIS EXCELLENCY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL IN COUNCIL.
speechtext: Sometimes it is, and I suppose it should be in all cases. I want it to be understood that if we sell at $1 an acre, as we sometimes do, it is because there has been a substantial fulfilment of the requirements but not a legal fulfilment of the requirements. We sell at that minimum price because the statute absolutely prohibits the issue of a patent unless the evidence is there that the duties have been fulfilled.

subtopic: HIS EXCELLENCY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL IN COUNCIL.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I want to say a word or two along general lines in support of the remarks of my hon. friend from Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff). I think I would not be doing justice to the administration of this department if I did not repeat some of the things I said before six o'clock as to the impartiality with which the department is administered. I have probably written, not a few hundreds, but a few thousands of times, in behalf of homesteaders and settlers to the Department of the Interior, and my most serious criticism of that department is that to my mind there is not sufficient leniency shown to the homesteader and settler. As to discrimination between man and man or as to -any consideration of political views and opinions, I have never seen anything of the kind in any single case. The only case that has ever come under my personal observation where the department held a court investigation, was the case of a warm personal friend and supporter. There was some doubt as to whether or not he had actually fulfilled all the requirements of the law as to the residence duties. There was no question about his cultivation duties, because he had broken some 140 acres out of a quarter-section and had cropped this land for a number of years. But, there were contradictory statements of the neighbours. This man, who is a good, substantial citizen, although he claimed to have performed sufficient resident duties on his homestead was not able to furnish absolutely conclusive proof thereof, with the result that what, to my mind, was a very severe sentence was passed upon him. He was asked by the department to go back upon the homestead and perform his residence duties over again. I have brought that case to the attention of the department, I do not know what their action will be, but I am Mr. OLIVER.
free to say that it is the only case of a court investigation that has come under my personal investigation. The man is a Liberal, a supporter of mine, but that had absolutely nothing to do with the 'consideration of his case. The witnesses whom he called, while giving it as the best of their knowledge and belief that he had performed sufficient residence, were not able to give days and dates, with the result that he did not obtain his patent when he made application for it, and, as a result of the investigation, he is compelled to go back upon the land. But while taking this position and while defending the administration of the department in so far as the question of partiality and impartiality is concerned, I am free to say that there are some features of the Dominion Lands Act and some features of the administration of the Act, that to my mind bear somewhat heavily upon the homesteader. Mind you, that with all the authority and responsibility of the Department -of the Interior and of the government in connection with the public lands of western Canada, neither the department nor the government should view or consider themselves in the light of proprietors. Neither the department nor this government are the proprietors of our western lands; they are simply the administrators. The lands belong to the people, and while a certain standard must undoubtedly be maintained, the rules and regulations of the department should be so framed as not to make the required duties too burdensome, too onerous, and too much of a hardship to the individual homesteader or settler. Men go thirty or forty miles away from the railway, and in days gone by many men have gone 150 miles, and even more, and homesteaded under our homestead regulations and laws.
These men who have to transport over those distances their furniture, the lumber with which to build their houses, their supplies from the nearest market and their produce to the nearest market, are entitled to every consideration, and the homestead conditions, instead of being such as to make it difficult for these men, the honest men, the sincere men, who desire to live on the land, -ought to make his duties as light and easy as possible. Western members realize the great difficulties with which homesteaders are confronted. Men of some means who take up homesteads or purchased land can obtain for themselves even in their homestead days many of the comforts which they have enjoyed in the older parts of Canada or in other countries, but many of those who go into western Canada have but limited means and perhaps large families, and the struggle that some of these homesteaders pass through in the three years before they obtain their homestead patent has in many cases been a thing pitiable to consider. It

is this aspect of the homesteader's life that I am bringing to the attention of th.e minister. The officers of the department ought to be imbued with this spirit of the homesteaders' life and every rule and regulation laid down by the minister for the direction of his officers and for the administration of the Lands Act should have in consideration this feature of the settler's life.
I wish to point out one or two features of the present administration of the homestead rules and regulations which I think might fairly be considered. Take for instance the homestead year. The law says that the homestead year is a year from the date of entry or from the commencement of residence. There may be cases where men have put in their residence and where the six months does not correspond absolutely with either of these periods. To my mind the spirit and the intention of the Domin-on Lands Act is that the man puts in six months' residence in each of three consecutive periods of 12 months is fulfilling the spirit of the law. I wish to call attention to the ease of the njan who performed his residence duties by living on purchased land. I suppose that that provision was put in the Dominion Lands Act to enable the man who wished not only to homestead but to purchase land to make his selection of which land he would live upon, whether it would be on the homestead	or on the purchased	land.
What we want in the west is settlers, men who will settle on the land and will cultivate it, not speculators, not men who take up a homestead in order by hook or by crook to lead the department at the end of three years to believe they have performed sufficient duties to entitle them to patents. We want actual settlers and if a man resides on purchased land instead of on his homestead^ and fulfils his residence and cultivation duties faithfully, even if he has only paid 50 cents an acre on that purchase land, surely he has fulfilled the requirements of the Act. The department does not hold that view. I cannot understand how it is possible to make an arbitrary decision as to what constitutes ownership of land. I do not think that the payment of 95 per cent or 99 per cent of the purchase price constitutes ownership any more than the payment of 5 per cent. So long as the man who has sold the land is content to give a contract for that land to the purchaser and is satisfied with the way in which the purchaser is living up to the conditions of that contract it would appear to me to be a fair proposition that the department would leave that question to be settled between the man who sold the land nd the man who purchased it.
I quite realize that the regulations are made fairly strict in order to prevent fraud on the part of those who would obtain patents for land without having performed sufficient residence, cultivation and other duties, but there is a possibility of leaning too far in the other direction, and, for the sake of hunting down the guilty, making the innocent man suffer. My view of the administration of the Lands Department is that it would be better to let one guilty man escape than to have 99 innocent men bear a heavy burden simply to prevent the one guilty man from getting away with a homestead quarter-section without having performed sufficient duties.	_ _
I simply wish to impress on_ the minister that the spirit of the administration and of the rules and regulations of the department should be one of sympathy with the homesteader, and that where it is possible to show leniency, leniency should be shown in.the interpretation of the law.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: HIS EXCELLENCY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL IN COUNCIL.
speechtext:
I quite accept the criticism of my hon. friend (Mr. Neely), and I appreciate the spirit in which it is made. I would not wish to think that_ a department so closely affecting the life of the western country was not the subject of consideration by those who have western interests at heart, and, of course, if a thing receives consideration that consideration cannot by any possibility always be favourable. I agree with my hon. friend that it would be a mistake for the government to consider itself as proprietor of the western lands. It is only the administrator of the lands in trust for the people of Canada, and particularly for the people who are going to become the occupiers. No man in this House and few outside of it know of their own knowledge the condition of the homesteader, the difficulties he has to overcome, and what might be called the tragedy of homesteading better than I do. No one has greater sympathy for the homesteader than I have, but in administering this trust there must be consideration of its purpose which is to secure not only the cultivation but the occupation of the land. That is the principle underlying the homestead Act. It is not enough that the land shall be occupied, or cultivated temporarily; the purpose is to secure permanent residence and any administration that lost sight of that ultimate purpose would not and could not be satisfactory. There is properly an insistence upon residence on the land because that is the main condition of the ownership of the land without payment of a price. It is of little account to the people of Canada if the land once passes out of public ownership, though every acre of it were brought under cultivation, unless it becomes in fact as well as in name a land of homesteads 1 with citizens in occupation of these home-

steads. Every consideration is given to the man who by his conduct indicates that he intends to become a permanent occupant of the land. The best evidence that the law and administration is satisfactory to the vast majority of those who iare in occupation of the land is the fact that their numbers are increasing from year to year The man who makes the complaint is the man who is not willing to fulfil all the conditions that are imposed upon him, and this man is in an insignificant minority as compared with the large majority of settlers who find the regulations absolutely satisfactory to them, and who become owners of the land and establish citizenship in the country. It is essential that there shall be continuity of settlement, and the man who holds a homestead without occupation of that homestead is not doing what is fair by his neighbours, who depend upon his being on his land to keep up the good of the neighbourhood. It is because of this that the law is framed as it is, and that we have insisted more strongly in recent than in former years upon fulfilment of the actual conditions. In justice to the legitimate settler who is on the land and fulfilling his duties his neighbour must do the_ same thing. It is true we do extend leniency and that we consider the requirements of individual eases, but it is also true that when you do grant leniency outside the ordinary routine you at once raise the question of discrimination, and those who have not required any leniency to be extended to them are apt to consider that the man who gets it is getting an unfair advantage. The large majority of cases where men have needed leniency and have not got it are due to the objections of their neighbours. The department, of its own motion, has hardly ever cancelled a man's entry; every cancellation is made on the application of some other man who says he wants that land. The difficulties we have in administration are not difficulties between the government and the settler, but between settler and settler. What we have to guard against more than anything else is to allow the idea to get into the minds of settlers that one can get an advantage which the other cannot. I find that people will quarrel more about the trifling advantage which one man in a settlement is supposed to have got than about something of real importance to the whole community. There will be more letters written to the department complaining that some men have got a little extra advantage than there would be if a real hardship were inflicted on the whole settlement. The very complaint which my friend from Qu'Appelle has made with regard to this man Bradley is an evidence in point. Bradley paid $5 an acre for his land, he did certain duties, he paid what other people have paid, but my hon. friend thinks Mr. OLIVER.
there has been some discrimination in his case-it could not have been a very great discrimination-and he thinks that a serious wrong has been done. I am not prepared to say that everything was right, even in that very case, but a thing of that kind will reflect more discredit on the department than possibly anything _ else which has occurred; and that is simply due to the fact that we dealt with that case leniently. My sympathy is absolutely with the settler. The administration of our land should be absolutely in their interest. But when leniency is asked, that means discrimination, and discrimination means a grievance in the minds of those who dr>
not require leniency and consequently do not ask for it.

subtopic: HIS EXCELLENCY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL IN COUNCIL.
speechtext:
In order to illustrate what I mean by a little more leniency being exercised on certain occasions, let me give one case I had to deal with. Two men, father and son, made homestead entries at a sub-agency and got their receipts. It is true that printed on the receipt in red ink were the words that the receipt was not absolute until the case was reported to the head office. But these men were foreigners, Frenchmen, who did not read-English. The son could not speak English at all, and the father very slightly. The entry was made at the sub-agency of Weyburn. Np doubt the sub-agent told the men thdy would have to wait until the papers went into Estevan before they would be absolutely certain that they would get their homestead, but these men did not understand English and they thought they had an absolute entry. The son got a homestead and the father, who had homesteaded already, purchased a pre-emption and paid $160 beside the $10 fee. They went out and broke up thirty acres and built a shanty before they became aware that one of these quarter-sections had already been entered. _ That quarter-section was the homestead which the son had improved. They did not speak English and consequently could not be made to understand. They came back to Weyburn and went to a lawyer, and the lawyer wrote to me. I went to the department and the case I put before the department was simply this. They said: We will give up the land if we get paid for the -work done. That is usually what is done. The government in granting, the re-entry, would make the man pay for the improvement, but the son said:	My father and I live together, we
must homestead close together, and there is no use of my going twenty miles further and taking another homestead unless my father can go there too and purchase a homestead alongside of me. The department insisted that under the regulations the $160 paid on account of the purchased homestead could not be refunded for a year, and in spite of all I could do-and

the father was a good supporter of mine-I could not get the department to allow that $160 to be refunded at once or applied on another purchased homestead. The father could not get his $160 back and could not take up another purchased homestead until he got it back, so that he and his son were prevented during a whole year from getting another entry. These are the regulations, no doubt, but it is a simple case in which the department should exercise leniency in administering these regulations. I do not think there is any regulation on earth that should compel a man to stay idle a whole year because $160 of His money is in the hands of the government and he cannot get it back. That is a case in which I claim the regulations work absolute injustice, and all I ask is a little bit of common horse sense applied to each individual case, and have each case dealt with on its merits. That man should have been allowed to have his $160 credited on the second purchased homestead even if the son and the father were both absolutely in the wrong. I am not saying that they were, for it is quite possible that the sub-agent made a mistake, but even if they were, leniency should have been exercised and the regulations should not have been allowed to interfere with a bona fide settler settling on his land.

subtopic: HIS EXCELLENCY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL IN COUNCIL.
speechtext: Can the minister give offhand any information as to what extent these irregularities in making application for homesteads, to. which the applicants are not entitled, have been carried on? I do not think they can have been to any great extent.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: HIS EXCELLENCY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL IN COUNCIL.
speechtext: I am afraid there has been a good deal of it, but of course all the cases we have dealt with have been published in the * Gazette ' and the number is not very large. I am afraid, however, that there are a good many which have not come to our attention. There is, I am afraid, carelessness in dealing with these matters, and a lack of consideration on the part of people in many cases which is not creditable. I introduced the purchased homestead preemption in the Land Act of 1908 in order that a person who had exhausted his homestead right could get legally another chance, and that no doubt did relieve the situation to a very great degree.

subtopic: HIS EXCELLENCY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL IN COUNCIL.
speechtext:
We have been dealing so far with the applicants for homesteads whose irregularities got them into trouble, and in some cases into jail. This year I have had a number of cases similar to the one of which I intend to give as an illustration to-night. And I am not presenting this case because I have had any trouble with the officials of the department. On the contrary in everything I have had to do with the department, I have found
the officials very courteous. They have never in any way refused recognition or consideration. But this is a case in which the officials to my mind have not given very satisfactory explanation to me, or to the parties for whom I have been trying to get an explanation. As I said, we have thus far been dealing with the applicant. But there seems to be in the case which I wish to put on 'Hansard' a fault on the part of the department. In the first case, the applicant is at fault, and the applicant has to suffer. But in the case to which I wish to refer, the department is at fault, and yet again, the applicant has to suffer. That does not seem fair. They call it an error. Well, let me read this case which I have referred to. Here is a letter addressed to myself and dated Cartwright, December 31, 1910.
iRe S.W. 5-37-9 W. 2nd.
Mr. Elijah Owens of this place has called to see me with reference to the above lands. It appears that he went west in the early part of the year and after a great deal of trouble and expense homesteaded the above quarter. The Land Office received his money and issued their usual interim receipt, &c. Subsequently Mr. Owens was informed that the south half of this quarter was patented on the 31st of December, 1907, to the Canadian Northern railway, and advised that if he was not satisfied with the eighty acres left, his entry would be cancelled. His main grievance is that the Land Office should have known of this and prevented him from taking the land after having incurred the expense necessary to homestead. Mr. Owens advises me that his travelling expenses locating the land amounted to $50. He had five acres broken on same at $1 per acre, making $20. He paid an entry fee of $10; his whole expenses being $80. You will see that this means quite a loss to Mr. Owens, as he does not want an eighty acre farm and will have to abandon same.
Now, I claim that in this case, the department made a mistake. Mr. Owens went to a great deal of trouble to go west and homestead this quarter-section. He did his breaking and fulfilled all the requirements; but later, was informed that half of this quarter-section had been patented to the Canadian Northern railway. The minister (Mr. Oliver) being familiar with the west will know that eighty acres will be practically of no use to the man and that it will be better for him to give up the quarter, and all that he asks is that he be refunded his expenses, because of the error of the department. And here is the answer of the department.
Ottawa, January 20, 1911.
Dear Sir,-With reference to the letter to you from Mr. John D. Loughlin, in re S.W. 1 of 5-37-9 W. 2nd, I beg to state that there is no provision in the Dominion Lands Act under which the department would have authority to grant the compensation asked for by Mr. Owens



I think that is along the lines on which hon. gentlemen opposite have been talking. It is pretty hard to get over the explanation made by the minister that you must have some law, and hold to that law, or somebody will be saying that you have been partial. I quite understand that.
-on the ground that he was granted entry for the above described land in error, the south half of the quarter-sectjon having been patented to the Canadian Northern Railway. Mr. Owens has been advised that if he did not wish to retain the available 80 acres as a homestead his entry would be cancelled and a refund of the entry fee would be made to him. I may state that under section 15 of the Act authority is given to cancel an entry which may have been granted through error.
With regard to compensating Mr. Owens for the breaking performed by him, I beg to state that under the practice of the department a homesteader who obtains entry for land upon which improvements have been made is called upon to pay to the department the value of such improvements, which amount the minister may in his discretion pay to the person who placed same upon the land. If, therefore, the breaking

I call special attention to this.
-mentioned by Mr. Owens is upon that portion of the said S.W. \ of 5 which is available for entry, the value, if any, of the improvements would be collected should re-entry be granted.
Now, the minister (Mr. Oliver) made use of some splendid sentiments about justice between man and man, and said, as I understood him, that all cases were considered on their merits. That is the way I think they should be considered. Here is a case that, I think, should have been treated on its merits. As I said, I am not finding fault with the officials of the department; but I wish to bring this case, as I promised I would do, to the attention of the minister. Here is a case in which a man not only went to the trouble and expense of making a journey and taking up land, but also of doing some breaking on' the land. And he has lost the opportunity of getting his quarter-section. I believe that Mr. Owens should receive back from the department that $80. I understand the department to say that they have no fund from which they could make such a payment. But they have all the funds there are in connection with the government; and, if the error is theirs, if, in the first place, you are going to say that the man who makes an error, has to suffer the penalty, why should not the department, when it makes an error, suffer the penalty? This is a sample of at least three or of four cases that I have had during the present session. I believe this is a case to which the minister should give some consideration; and I do believe that Mr. Owens should re-Mr. SCHAFiFNER.
ceive back his $80. Even then, he will have suffered a loss.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: HIS EXCELLENCY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL IN COUNCIL.
speechtext: There is no doubt, this gentleman has suffered a hardship, and because of the error of the department. It is also a fact that provision has not been made for dealing with such a case, and, therefore, we are limited in our dealings to just exactly what has been done. We could collect the amount of the improvements from any subsequent entrant and pay them to the gentleman who made the improvements. But we should have no warrant for dealing with travelling expenses, and I think myself it would be very doubtful policy to go so far as to pay travelling expenses in such a case. It might be argued that Mr. Owens had incurred travelling expenses looking over land, but there was other land in that part of the country as well as the land he took. His expenses might be arranged in some way that, if he took another homestead we could give it to him without incurring travelling expenses or something of that kind. I am satisfied it would not be possible, under the circumstances, to meet the demand for travelling expenses.

subtopic: HIS EXCELLENCY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL IN COUNCIL.
speechtext: They might be cut out.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: HIS EXCELLENCY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL IN COUNCIL.
speechtext: We must admit that we were in fault. If it were possible to give the gentleman a consideration-as sometimes has been done-as I say, there is no fund from which to draw, but sometimes where we have wronged an individual iri that way we try to make it up to him should he take a subsequent entry by some consideration in the matter of duties or something of that kind. But that is the only way that the regulations allow us to deal with it.

subtopic: HIS EXCELLENCY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL IN COUNCIL.
speechtext: Could not that be changed? Is it a fair regulation?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: HIS EXCELLENCY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL IN COUNCIL.
speechtext:
It may be that it would be proper to make a change to meet such cases. But there have been very, very few of them, and the loss is not a,very serious loss. If the gentleman is taking land elsewhere, we might meet his wishes in some way in regard to fulfilment of duties, or in some other way that would be satisfactory to him.
Mr. SCHAFFNER, Will the minister take this letter and write me as to what will be done?

subtopic: HIS EXCELLENCY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL IN COUNCIL.
speechtext:
Before this item carries, I would like to bring to the notice of the minister some details in the Auditor General's Report of last year. I have referred to two of the employees of the department, and have suggested to the minister that if he wanted the confidence of the general public he had better let them go.

In the Auditor General's Report, K-53, I find a reference to one R. E. A. Leech. He is put down here as an inspector of agencies at Brandon, with a salary of $3,000 a year and expenses. Is that the same Leech that is famous in Manitoba, or infamous, according to the point of view, since 1904, who is called the Thin Red Line Leech?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: HIS EXCELLENCY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL IN COUNCIL.
speechtext: I think this gentleman has been called the Red Line Leech?

subtopic: HIS EXCELLENCY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL IN COUNCIL.
speechtext: Might I ask how did a gentleman with a nickname of that kind come to be appointed by a government that is desirous of getting the confidence of the public?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: HIS EXCELLENCY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL IN COUNCIL.
speechtext: The gentleman was appointed before I became minister, I found him in the position, and I must say that I have found him a very efficient and faithful servant.

subtopic: HIS EXCELLENCY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL IN COUNCIL.
speechtext: I am glad to know that the minister finds him efficient and faithful. But there are one or two things concerning him I wish to mention. He has a salary of $3,000 a year. Then there is an item for board, lodging and horse feed, $1,073.15. Would the minister tell me what is meant here by horse feed?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: HIS EXCELLENCY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL IN COUNCIL.
speechtext: I could not offhand give my hon. friend the detailed information. I understand that Mr. Leech's accounts are now before the Public Accounts Committee, and I am sure that every detail possible will be arrived at by that committee. In a general way, I can answer the question about horse feed. Mr. Leech's duties require him to visit the different land agenda in Saskatchewan and Manitoba. In addition he is from time to time employed in taking evidence in questions of the fulfilment of homestead duties, and in many such cases he has to drive to the locality in which the investigation is held and requires to have a horse.

speechtext:
In looking further, I find letters in regard to this same man written by the Auditor General which show that he does not have the same confidence in Mr. Leech which is now expressed by the minister. On K-126. I find a letter written from the Audit Office in Ottawa, dated February 22,	1910, signed by J.
Fraser, Auditor General. Referring to Inspector Leech's travelling expenses. He says:
I have before me the expense accounts of Mr. R. A. E. Leech, inspector of agencies, for the period included between April 1 and October 31, 1909, and would ask your attention to the following remarks thereon:
1. In no instance does Mr. Leech make use of return tickets on the railways, but charges single fare in all cases. While on some of his trips, which are of a roundabout nature, return tickets could not well be made use of, still there are others on which a saving might have been made by the purchase of return tickets. For instance, there are about twenty trips between Brandon and Winnipeg for which $1 each way is charged. The return fare should be only about $6.70, which would have made a saving of $1.30 on each round trip. Again, on a trip to Ottawa and return, $33.80, the ordinary single fare, is charged each way. The regular return ticket from Winnipeg to Ottawa, however, is $59.45, so that a saving of $8.15 might have been effected on this trip. There are other trips on which, I think, return tickets might have been advantageously made use of.
I would make the suggestion to the minister that if there is any doubt in the mind of the watchdog of the treasury, the Auditor General, that any employee of this government is not absolutely honest in his accounts, a very much better method to follow than that at present followed would be to compute for a certain time the average expense and have an arrangement made with the different railways so that passes could be had and the average passenger rate paid straight from the government to the railway companies, thus removing any inducement in the way of an official who was mistrusted by the Auditor General to bring any onprobium on his name either rightly or wrongly.
3. With reference to livery hire, it appears that Mr. Leech is under a misapprehension with respect to the necessity for vouchers. He states that, according to his information,

livery vouchers are required only when the bill amounts to a considerable sum. In the November statement no single charge is for more than one day's livery hire, the highest for which is eight dollars. Eight dollars, however, would represent a very heavy day's drive, or the drive of a day and the good part of a night. I am advising Mr. Leech that sub-vouchers are required for all payments for livery hire.
4 and 5. With respect to meals on dining cars, Mr. Leech informs me that when he commenced work for the department and for some time afterwards, the price of meals was $1, which only required the keeping track of the number of meals in connection with his expenses. When these rates were changed by the railway companies it was only for the purpose of increasing their charges, and now it is a very poor meal one can get by limiting the price to $1, but as it is more convenient he has adhered to the old plan, although the meals have cost him considerably more.
To conclude, I might say that I have instructed Mr. Leech to bear your remarks very carefully in mind in future, and to make out his accounts in accordance therewith. I trust the explanations given with respect to the accounts already rendered will prove sufficient.
I am, sir, your obedient servant,

headed:

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
I would like the minister's special attention to this, because I think if is very important. The letter I read a moment ago was answered in a certain way by the Deputy Minister. This one is not answered and I would like the answer to-night.
Audit Office,
Ottawa, March 11, 1910.
Sir,-I beg to call your attention to certain inconsistencies between the fares charged by Mr. R. E. A. Leech, inspector of agencies, in his expense accounts and the amounts paid the railway companies for tickets supplied to him on transportation orders.
Order No. 1036 is for a single ticket from Calgary to Edmonton, delivered Mr. Leech by the Canadian Pacific railway ticket agent at Calgary on October 15, 1908. Order No. 1361, dated October 16, 1908, is for a single ticket from Edmonton to Regina, delivered Mr. Leech by the agent of the Canadian Northern railway. This order is stamped by the Canadian Northern Railway at Edmonton on October 23, 1908. On referring to Mr. Leech's accounts for the month of October, 1908, it would appear he arrived in Calgary from Banff on October 15

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
That is the day that he got the ticket from the Canadian Pacific railway agent.
-that he remained in Calgary until the 17tli, on which date he left for Brandon direct, charging in his account a single fare ticket from Calgary to Brandon. He returned to Calgary again on the 19th, and on the 21st went back to Brandon. On October 23, the date on which the order was stamped at Edmonton, Mr. Leech appears to have been at Medicine Hat, on his way from Calgary to Brandon.
We, on this side of the House, recognized his capacity for taking care of personation, but wre did not know that he could be in two places at one time in his own person.
Order No. 1041 is for a single ticket from Calgary to Edmonton, delivered to Mr. Leech ,by the Canadian Pacific railway agent at Calgary on April 27, 1909. Mr. Leech's expense account shows that while he was at Calgary on April 27, 1909, he left on that date for Regina and did not go up to Edmonton.
Surely this is something that the minister ought to take into consideration.
Order No. 425 is for a single ticket from Regina to Prince Albert, supplied Mr. Leech by the agent of the Canadian Northern railway on May 10, 1909, Mr. Leech's expense account shows that he arrived in Regina from Brandon on May 10, that he stayed in Regina until the following day, when he left for Winnipeg. He does not appear to have gone ti Prince Albert at this time at all.
Surely that is something else for the minister to take into his consideration. The department was paying his way into

a different point at the same time as he had a ticket to go somewhere else, both tickets being paid for by the people.
Order No. 2152 is for a single ticket from Regina to Prince Albert, supplied to Mr. Leech by the agent of the Canadian Northern railway at Brandon on July 21, 1909. According to Mr. Leech's expense account he arrived in Brandon from Areola on July 16 and remained at Brandon until July 23

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
The ticket he had got from Regina to Prince Albert was dated July 21.
-on which date he went to Winnipeg. He does not appear to have been at Prince Albert any time during the month of July.
Another case of personation. I am glad to notice that the nod of the minister is so emphatic that he must agree with me that Mr. Leech is an adept at impersonation.
Order No. 444 is for a single ticket from Regina to Prince Albert, delivered Mr. Leech by the agent of the Canadian Northern railway at Regina on July 30, 1909. Prom his expense account, Mr. Leech appears to have arrived in Regina from Banff on July 30, and to have proceeded the same date to Brandon, and not to Prince Albert.
He had a ticket for Prince Albert for which the people paid at the same time as he had obtained a ticket presumably for himself to go to Brandon.
Mr. Leech should have to explain why he issued transportation orders in his own name in the above cases, when his expense accounts show that he was travelling in a totally different direction. It is probable that the tickets supplied on the transportation orders in question were not for his own use, but for the use of other officials. If such was the case the name of the official using the ticket supplied should have been endorsed on the transportation order, or still better, the transportation order should have been issued, not in Mr. Leech's name, but in the name of the official actually using the ticket. A full explanation of the circumstances under which each order was issued should be furnished by Mr. Leech.
I am, sir, your obedient servant,
J. FRASER, A.Gn.
The Deputy Minister of the Interior.
That letter was written from the Audit Office, March 11, 1910, and as far as I can learn, no answer has yet been returned to it. I would like an explanation now.

speechtext:
I notice there is no answer in the Auditor General's Report to that letter. The reason is that there was some delay in answering and the answer which should have appeared in the Auditor General's Report was too 'late for insertion. I . have here a copy of the answer to that letter and I shall place it on ' Hansard.' It reads:
Dear Mr. Fraser,-I am in receipt of your letter of the 30th ultimo, in which you draw attention to the fact that you have never received a reply to your letter of the 11th of March last, relating to certain transportation orders issued by Mr. R. E. A. Leech, inspector ot Dominion Lands agencies, which appear to conflict with his expense accounts. In reply, I beg to say that you will doubtless recall that in the year 1908, Mr. Leech was placed in charge of a general seed distribution which was conducted in the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta. It was originally contemplated to bring employees of this department from various Land Offices to assist Mr. Leech in his work, but owing to the unprecedented demand for seed grain of that year and the extent of the work involved in distributing it to needy settlers, it was found necessary to employ a great many temporary men to assist in various capacities. Some of them were sent out on special trips to various points and in such cases were given transportation orders by Mr. Leech in his name or the tickets were secured on Mr. Leech's order and given to them. In no instance, however, were such orders used except on government business.
I understand that Mr. Reid of your office lately called on Mr. Leech and went into this matter fully. I presume that probably you have his report ere this.
Yours very truly,
(Sgd.) W. W. CORY.
Deputy Minister.
John Fraser, Esq., Auditor General.

subtopic: INSPECTOR LEECH'S EXPENSES, INCONSISTENCIES BETWEEN FARES CHARGED AND TRANSPORT ORDERS ISSUED.
speechtext:
That is satisfactory, except that the department had to be jogged five or six months after and asked for a statement with regard to it. I shall read another letter from Mr. Fraser with regard to the same Mr. Leech, with reference to his sleeping and parlour car charges:
Audit Office,
Ottawa, March 14, 1909.
Sir,-In my examination of the accounts of Mr. R. E. A. Leech, inspector of agencies, for the seven months included between April 1 and October 31, 1909, it appears to me'that the charges made by him for accommodation on sleeping cars and on parlour cars are considerably in excess of the advertised rates for such services. I inclose herewith a statement showing the various charges made by lum, the correct amounts, as nearly as I could determine them, and the apparent overcharges. In making out this statement, I have been guided, as far as possible, by the amounts advertised by the transportation companies. In other cases, however, I have been guided by the charges made by other officials for similar services. In a few cases it was difficult to determine whether the trip was made during the day or by night. In such cases I have been guided, as far as possible, by the charges for meals on the dining cars, as during the night these cars are not open. The amounts allowed by me, in the column headed 'correct charges' are subject to modification. Mr. Leech, however, should be asked to justify each charge made by him and to refund any overcharge.
When the Auditor General seriously makes a statement of this kind and absolutely says that Leech has been overcharge

ing the department, I think it is time for the department to seriously take the matter into consideration and ascertain the facts. Either Mr. Fraser or his clerical staff is incompetent, or Mr. Leech is dishonest. In saying that I do not wish to say anything detrimental to the capacity and capability of the Auditor General and his staff.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: INSPECTOR LEECH'S EXPENSES, INCONSISTENCIES BETWEEN FARES CHARGED AND TRANSPORT ORDERS ISSUED.
speechtext:
That letter is replied to on the following page as follows:
Department of the Interior,
Ottawa, June 10, 1910.
Dear Mr. Fraser,-Referring to your letter of March It last, with reference to the accounts of Mr. R. E. A. Leech, inspector of Dominion Land agencies, relating particularly to the sleeping car charges, I beg to say that I am now in receipt of an explanation from this official. He says, in effect, that he has always found it difficult to determine i' hether all the charges are in accordance with the sleeping car schedules. He has only recently been able to borrow a Canadian Pacific railway official sleeping car schedule, but even from this he has not been able to determine the rates in many cases. Those which the schedule shows plainly, however, indicate that his charges are correct, except a charge made nn April 7, Winnipeg to Nokomis, $4. In this case the through rate, as shown on the nnhedule, is $3, but if the trip had been broken or sleeper had been engaged, say from Winnipeg to Elkhorn and then from Elkhorn to Nokomis, the cost would have been $4.
I inclose you herewith a statement from Mr. Leech showing you the charges as he has been able to verify them from the schedules, but the schedules are somewhat intricate, and he has only given figures where there was no question as to what the charge should be. I trust you will find the explanation satisfactory.
I am, sir, your obedient servant,

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext:
The Auditor General.
There follows a statement of affairs made by Mr. Leech, taken from the schedule and compared with the schedule of fares and Mr. Leech makes the assertion that the correct fares have been charged.

What authority had Leech to issue those orders to any other individual? It seems to me that he takes a great deal of authority upon himself. In Manitoba, to our dissatisfaction and discomfort, he took on himself authority to do what he saw fit with the voters' lists. Now, I understand he takes authority to issue to other agents travelling orders which I am led to believe are simply Jrom a little book of coupons on which? the ticket agent issues tickets. It would only take an hour or two to get an order from the minister to issue these transportation orders. Mr. Leech manages to carry on things in a high handed way and apparently he has some hold on the government Mr. CAMPBELL.
which enables him to do just as he pleases, and in his case the government dare not say their souls are their own. He draws a salary of $3,000 a year which he augments to $7,000 by other expenses. I believe the government could get a competent and honest man to discharge Mr. Leech's duties for a far less salary. And yet, the government goes on employing him from year to year notwithstanding that all these doings of his have been brought to their attention. It is time the minister should call a halt on Mr. Leech and investigate his transactions.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Leech was a commissioner with full responsibility to see that the seed grain got out and no technicality in regard to the issue of transportation or anything else was to stand in his way. It was a case of delivering the goods, and Leech delivered the goods in time, to the satisfaction of the people, and to the very great benefit of the country at large. He could not have done so had he been hampered by a requirement to appeal to Ottawa for issue of transportation when it was required. It is true that Mr. Leech is an expensive official. It is true he has a high salary and that his travelling expenses are very high, but I do not think they amount to more than is paid to other men in private life who are engaged in duties that are not any more responsible and that are not discharged with any greater ability. Although I did not appoint Mr. Leech I want to say on his behalf that his services as inspector of Dominion Land agencies, and in the position we have frequently placed him in as acting as a sort of court in case of dispute as to homestead duties', and particularly in the administration of the seed grain distribution, have been eminently satisfactory so far as my knowledge goes, and I take this opportunity of saying so.
He charges a dollar fare from Brandon to Winnipeg and there is no such fare.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Are you complaining that he doe3 not charge enough?
He charges 50 cents too much each time.
The Canadian Pacific Rail-rvay folder gives the charge from Brandon to Winnipeg at 50 cents, and every time Mr. Leech charges double the legal fare.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I know he is an expensive man.
He is worse than that, he is a dishonest man.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
That can be threshed out before the Public Accounts Committee better than here and it is open to my hon. friend to prove M*. Leech's dishonesty if dis-
5614
I /

honest he is. He is certainly at their mercy to make what they can out of him in the Public Accounts Committee, and I assure them he gets no protection from me.
If he travels by night in a pullman car from Brandon to Winnipeg the fare is two dollars, but in the day time the fare is 50 cents, and he apparently charges one dollar.

If the department had the public interest at heart they would have asked Mr. Leech before now to supply the names of the persons he employed in this case of emergency. The minister says that Leech was aide to deliver the goods, and we all know he is a pretty handy man at delivering the goods, particularly on one occasion when he delivered the goods to the electors of Manitoba.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That was the time he failed to deliver the goods.
He did not fail to erase the names of elector^ who were entitled to vote.
What is the matter with your law in Alanitoba?

The law is all right, but this Dominion official was all wrong. It is time the government took means to inquire into this man's actions more closely and that his services were dispensed with. That is my opinion of the honesty and efficiency of that gentleman no matter what the opinion of the Minister of the Interior is.

The Auditor General's report makes out that in 83 trips during 7 months there was an overcharge made, and Air. Leech only attempts to explain 23 of them. Until he has cleared himself of the charge that he lias been systematically over-charging and putting the balance in his pocket Mr. Leech should not be allowed to act in the semi-judicial capacity he is constantly called upon to fill.

I would like to ask the hon. minister how it was that Mr. AIcLean, who is employed in Winnipeg at $5 a day, was sent out just a month before the last local election in order to distribute scrip and was paid $10 a day extra. I cannot find out where he was distributing any scrip at all, but he was supposed to be a heeler for the Liberal party at the local election. It was in October that he was out doing that work, and he should have been paid at the end of October or in November. But he was not paid until the 1st of Alarch following. By delaying payment, the item never appeared in the Auditor General's Report until a year and a half after the work had been done. The result was that the government were paying this man $5 per day in Winnipeg while he was absent 177
from his work, and $10 a day besides for working in the local elections of Saskatchewan and Alberta. And at the same time this man meets Leech who was travelling all over the province, and the stubs of the tickets will show that while he gave certificates say from Calgary to Edmonton, he was travelling from Calgary to Regina. The inference to be drawn is that he had a lot of political workers going around the country and paid by the department at Ottawa. It is all very fine for the minister to say to us: you can go before the Public Accounts Committee and prove what you say. But how can we prove it? Leech will swear that these men were employed to run out and examine somebody's farm or something of that kind. The Act was illegal, it was defrauding the country in an underhand way, and the Minister of the Interior must have instructed Leech and McLean to do that kind of work. Then the minister held the payments over from October until after the 1st of March. Why did he not pay the men at once? I ask the minister now to explain that transaction and clear it up if he can. Then if it should come before the Public Accounts Committee, we will have the minister's statement, and see if Leech and McLean will confirm it.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
With regard to Leech and
the tickets he issued to other people in his own name, I can only say that the case was one of urgency. A great deal of work had to be done in a short time, and it was important, not only to the individuals concerned, but the country at, large, that it should be done. Mr. Leech tried to exercise his judgment in these matters, and I am prepared to stand right behind him in that transportation. I do not wish to be understood that I am going to stand behind Leech in any investigation that shall be made in the Public Accounts Committee into all his financial transactions with regard to his own expenditures. If dishonesty can be shown against him, he will have to take the consequences; but so far as the issue of special transportation was concerned at the time of the issue of seed grain, I take the full responsibility. It was a case of urgency. Leech had full authority, and I have every confidence that what was done was done in the interests of the public. With regard to W. J. McLean, Whatever there may be against Leech as being a political worker, there is no such charge agains.t McLean. Mr. McLean was an old employee of the Hudson Bay Company, over 70 years of age. On account of his knowledge of the Indian language and character and his general desire to be employed, we gave Air. McLean this particular work of paying the Indian treaty money and taking evidence with regard to halfbreed scrip in the far northern country north of Prince Albert. The ordinary time of the year for paying treaty money was in



that month. McLean was paid by the two departments because he was working for the two. He was paid by the Indian Department for his work in paying out the treaty money, and by the Interior Department for taking evidence with regard to halfbreed scrip., The idea that Mr. McLean could under any circumstances be valuable politically is utterly preposterous.

The hon. minister has let the cat out of the bag. McLean is no political worker, but during the month before the local elections he was sent out with this treaty money. It was not so urgent months before to pay this treaty money, but it became very urgent within two or three weeks of the election. McLean did not go out to buy votes, but here are a lot of electors in a local'election who want their claims settled, and McLean was sent out to pay them. Is it not astonishing that for months previously the minister would not settle this claim, and just a month before the elections he sent out a good honest old gentleman, whom no one would suspect of being a political leader. He sent him out to get the evidence and see who had claims. Some of the claimants he did not pay. He did not pay until after the election, and then went out to find all those people who had claims. He did not mention politics, of course, but there was a man guiding him around who was known as a political heeler. The minister knows better than that. He says it was very urgent and that they had to be settled just then. Of course it was urgent to carry the election.
Did the Indians have votes in the election?

What about the halfbreeds? Have they not votes? They got scrip just the same as the Indians. The minister fixed the whole scheme and sent McLean just to get votes. He 6ent Leech out with seed grain of course, because of course that was necessary, but Leech was sent out when the local elections were going on. The minister should get up and acknowledge that the whole thing was a political scheme from start to finish. The men delivered the goods, there is no doubt about that; but they delivered them with money taken from the people of this country, illegally as I claim. The minister ban ease his conscience by saying that he did not go but himself buying votes; but it was an act he would not do in his private business, though in a public matter of this kind it is easy for him to settle his conscience if his conscience is at all pliable.

With regard to the items referred to by the Auditor General in his letter of transportation issued by Mr. Leech to some one else, I can readily understand that it might be absolutely justifiable' under the circumstances the minister Mr. OLIVER.
has just cited in the case of the distribution of seed grain, though I do not see why a man could not buy his ticket and charge it up to the department in the manner usually followed. But I have yet to learn- and I would like the minister to note this- of any part of the Northwest provinces which sow at the end of July or in October. Why, then, should grain be distributed for seed purposes at these dates? The minister will find that of these five cases only two were in April and May when seed grain possibly could have been used, and the others in July and October. The reason the minister alleged surely cannot be the correct one.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In regard to other times of the year, of course the same justification does not exist. I do not pretend to justify Mr. Leech issuing transportation under ordinary circumstances. But, as I have already said, so far as the seed grain distribution is concerned, I must stand by him in that.

I am not finding fault with that, but these are absolute charges brought by the Auditor General against this man Leech. One of these dates, as I have said, is October 23. There is no seed grain distributed then, unless it be winter wheat, and there was none grown in that part of the country at that time. And July 23, and July 30-you don't sow anything then.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There is no seed distribution at that time. I will inquire of Mr. Leech as to these. And, in the meantime, if the Public Accounts Committee are sitting on Mr. Leech, I can only advise them to go at him and find out for themselves. In the other cases, we will try to find out his explanation.

The minister is placing too much emphasis on the investigation about to take place before the Public Accounts Committee. I believe that all that has been done so far is to move foT the papers. Whether there will be an investigation or not will depend wholly upon the character of these papers. But, with the charges contained in the Auditor General's Report, the minister should riot have satisfied himself with a waiting action by the Public Accounts Committee, but should have investigated the accounts and had Mr. Leech on the carpet to make an explanation. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Lake) has referred to the fact that Mr. Leech could easily have verified the charges by looking up a Canadian Pacific railway-folder. But if we are to take Mr. Leech's word for it, we must take into consideration how difficult it is for him to secure one of these folders. Here is this great transcontinental line with its immense business; and Mr. Leech is in Winnipeg

*
In Brandon.

Yes, but he goes to Winnipeg sometimes in an election. And he would have us believe that it was three months before he could secure a folder, and then he had to borrow one. Mr. Cory's letter replying to the Auditor General is dated June 10, and begins ' Referring to your letter of March 14.' That is, it took until June 10, for this explanation to be forthcoming. And it proceeds:
I beg to say that I am now in receipt of an explanation from this official. He says, in effect, that he has always found it difficult to determine whether all the charges are in accordance with the sleeping car schedules. He has only recently been able to borrow a Canadian Pacific railway official sleeping car schedule, but even from this he has not been able to determine the rates in many cases.
How puerile that explanation is. It is ridiculous that we should be told, as a lot of intelligent men, that for three months he could not secure a Canadian Pacific railway folder in order to find the accuracy of these charges. I think an explanation should have been demanded of him by his superior officer, the Minister of the Interior, long ere this. In these large expenses, in addition to a large salary of $3,000 per annum, there is a chance, with a gentleman who does not bear the most enviable reputation, to get in small graft, and even large graft, by overcharging his expenses, unless the vouchers are forthcoming for everything expended. Mr. Leech's head office is in Brandon, but he appears periodically in Winnipeg, and usually at the time of an election. In the last provincial election he had business that kept him almost constantly, I am informed, in the city of Winnipeg. He used to be the provincial organizer for the Liberal party in the province of Manitoba, and it was understood that because of his services in that capacity that he was given his present position. No doubt, his knowledge of political affairs in that province was valuable to his party. I believe that in the provincial election in Saskatchewan, his services were needed, espcially in Regina. But he is not the only official who interests himself in that way. At page K-56 of the Auditor General's Report, we find the name of Mr. Ostrosky, who receives $100 a month and expenses, and who is a most active political agent. He came into my constituency during the late election and went through securing naturalization papers for the Galicians at no expense to them, of course, the money, no doubt, coming from the political party in whose interest he was acting. Now possibly the Minister of the Interior may be entirely ignorant of those circumstances. But whoever is responsible, this gentleman at any rate, who is an official of the Interior Department, has been very active during election time.

I draw this to the attention of the minister so that he may make inquiry into the circumstances himself. He has expressed himself more than once in this House as being opposed to his officials taking part in elections. But in regard to Mr. Leech's expenses, I hold that the Minister of the Interior should long ere this have made a personal investigation into the charges made against Mr. Leech, in view of the correspondence that we read in the Auditor General's Report.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not for a moment throw responsibility on the Public Accounts Committee for the proper conduct of the affairs of the Interior Department. It is quite proper, as the hon. gentleman has said, that the accounts which are investigated by the Auditor General should be investigated by the department, and I propose to see that that is done. I merely offered the suggestion to hon. gentlemen that by the Public Accounts Committee they had an independent means of arriving at all the facts in regard to these accounts.

It is now midnight, and it will take us hours to get through with Mr. Leech. I would ask, therefore, that the government allow us to adjourn.
Some resolutions reported.
On motion of Mr. Fielding, House adjourned at, 11.52 p.m.
